    mode: single
  dossier_skill:
    skill_id: dossier-generation
    name: Dossier generation
    path: 00_System/skills/dossier-generation.md
    instructions: "Uses: answer\n\nWrite the actual dossier in Markdown. Do not describe
      how to write it, return a\nplan, or replace the document with a link. These
      instructions govern dossier\nwriting only. The supporting skills remain independent.
      Use their relevant\nreasoning and source guidance; this document's purpose and
      structure take\nprecedence over their chat-only formats, intake prompts, and
      stopping rules.\nDo not run new research merely to refresh the dossier.\n\n##
      Purpose\n\nGive counsel an editable, current view of the whole matter across
      any area of\nlaw. Use the supplied matter records and saved research. Lead with
      the answer\nand the judgment needed. Be concise but retain the reasoning a lawyer
      needs.\nDo not add generic disclaimers or turn missing support into a refusal.\n\nThe
      North Star is the business's controlling question and objective, starting\nwith
      the original request and any explicit lawyer clarification or reframe.\nThe
      latest chat question is normally a supporting inquiry, not replacement\nscope.
      Answer the business question even when a later exchange is narrow.\nTest the
      premise behind the request. Explain when the evidence supports a\ndifferent
      answer, a changed route, or not proceeding. Do not force the facts\nto support
      the business's proposed solution or silently rewrite its question.\n\nAssess
      material issues from the current records and relevant history across\nall supplied
      matter conversations. The saved issue list is a starting point,\nnot a ceiling.
      Include a newly identified material issue in the Issues section,\nwith its source
      and effect on the business question. Use ordinary headings for\nissues without
      saved IDs; do not invent an ID or claim the issue list was changed.\nRead omitted
      passages through the captured-record reader when needed. Preserve\ntheir speaker,
      date, corrections and hypothetical scope. Do not claim that\navailable records
      were all read. Judge detail by its value to the business\nanswer and counsel's
      next decision, not a fixed depth-versus-breadth quota.\n\nOn a refresh, derive
      the current position again from the current records and\nsupported issue analysis.
      The prior dossier is fallible synthesis for continuity,\nnot a wording template
      or evidence that an activity is cleared. Keep useful\nreasoning, but replace
      conclusions and assumption labels that the current inputs\ndo not support. Preserve
      the recorded direction and decisions as records; explain\nseparately when this
      draft recommends a change. Retention of prior research means\nit stays accessible,
      not that its earlier conclusions must stay unchanged.\n\nWrite the general matter
      dossier, even when the conversation is exploring an\nalternative. The current
      direction stays the planning baseline. Recording a\nhypothetical in this document
      does not adopt it or change any reported fact.\n\n## Reading order\n\n1. A short
      title and **Current position**: answer the business question in a\n   short
      decision brief. Give the recommended course now, why it best serves\n   the
      objective, what can proceed, and what should wait or change. Name the\n   decisive
      conditions, not every information gap. Distinguish this draft's\n   recommendation
      from the accepted working view and any recorded decision.\n2. **Decision question**:
      reproduce the supplied controlling business question exactly. It\n   is the
      matter's scope, not a question for the model to replace.\n   If no question
      has been recorded, frame a provisional business question from\n   the original
      request; do not substitute the latest conversational subquestion.\n3. One **Issues**
      section covering EVERY supplied issue. Keep each issue's\n   stable identity
      with an invisible `<!-- issue:ISS-... -->` marker before its\n   heading. Do
      not substitute a second, different issue list.\n4. **Next actions**: a short,
      ranked work plan. For each action give the\n   deliverable, the result needed
      to proceed, the dependent decision or activity,\n   and the fallback if that
      result is not available. Order by dependencies and\n   time sensitivity, not
      merely the saved issue order. Reuse assigned work and\n   its recorded owner
      and date. When no assignment exists, suggest an owner\n   role and timing relative
      to a real milestone, clearly labeled **Proposed**.\n   Do not invent a person,
      commitment, legal deadline, or calendar date.\n   Distinguish a source-based
      deadline from a suggested working target.\n5. Brief links to available current
      work product, supporting records, and prior\n   revisions. Omit empty inventories
      and routine record housekeeping that does\n   not affect the decision. Do not
      paste the old dossier or superseded advice\n   into the body.\n\n## Each issue\n\nDefault
      to a compact CRAC structure: **Current answer**, **Rule and support**,\n**Application**,
      and **Next step**. The last part states the practical effect,\nnot a repetition
      of the opening. Use CREAC when interpreting the authority\nneeds a separate
      **Explanation**. Use IRAC only when the issue itself still\nneeds to be framed.
      Do not pad a section to meet a template.\n\nKeep work status separate from the
      legal answer. Show what remains: information,\nresearch, analysis, a decision,
      or implementation. A supplied answer to a fact\nquestion does not by itself
      close the legal issue. Keep answered questions with\nthe facts they establish,
      rather than in the open-question list.\n\nRetain prior analysis of issues untouched
      by the latest research. Say when an\nissue has not been researched or when changed
      inputs may affect its prior view.\nDepth on one issue must not make the other
      issues disappear.\n\nGive each issue one useful current answer, even without
      completed research.\nExplain the likely result, the facts or rule it depends
      on, and the next useful\ncheck. Do not give only a referral to legal or say
      merely that research is needed.\nMake the reasoning usable: identify the applicable
      actor, conduct, jurisdiction\nor contract, and the operative test. Apply each
      decisive condition to the known\nfacts. If a material fact is missing, explain
      the result on either side of that\nfact and recommend an interim course. A statement
      that something 'depends on\nthe terms' is incomplete unless it says which term
      matters and how it changes\nthe answer. Address a material exception or competing
      reading when it could\nchange the recommendation; do not invent one to fill
      a template.\n\nUse saved source passages to explain the rule and its material
      qualifications,\nwith the source and locator beside the proposition. A source
      title, URL, or\nopening excerpt alone is not the operative rule. Treat private
      agreements and\ncompany policies as those types of support, not public law.
      If no relevant\nauthority is saved, give the best conditional analysis and label
      that legal\npremise as unverified. State the precise research question once;
      do not repeat\n'not researched' in place of analysis or claim research happened
      in this run.\n\nConnect issues that affect the same decision. Explain what a
      proposed mitigation\nsolves, what it does not solve, and which dependency must
      be met first. Distinguish\na legal requirement from a recommended risk control
      or business preference.\nA possible way forward is not permission to proceed.
      Separating activities or\nmilestones does not establish that either is cleared;
      qualify the earlier step\nwhen its independent contractual or legal conditions
      are not established.\nThe application places full saved research in a disclosure
      under its issue;\ndo not create saved-research disclosures yourself, repeat
      old analysis, or add a\nsaved-answer appendix. Write the current synthesis;
      the application preserves\nthe original research separately.\n\n## Alternatives
      considered\n\nInclude this section when saved alternatives are supplied. Use
      one subsection\nper alternative, with its `<!-- alternative:SCN-... -->` marker
      and saved title.\nLabel it **Hypothetical — not adopted** (or archived, if the
      record says so).\nState its assumptions, how it helps or hinders the objective,
      added risks,\nissues it leaves unresolved, and the next action. Keep each alternative's\nworking
      note and attached test evidence within that alternative. Do not blend\nseparate
      proposals or treat a test assumption as an actual matter fact.\nInclude material
      dates, controls, and dependencies from the saved working note.\nLink the saved
      alternative. Do not infer acceptance or a recorded decision.\nFor each decisive
      condition, explain what the alternative changes and what still\napplies. A change
      in format, asset, actor, or channel does not itself remove a\npermission requirement
      or contractual restriction. If the saved terms do not\nsettle whether the restriction
      applies to the alternative, state that condition.\nDo not present uncertain
      exemption as the reason the fallback can proceed.\nCompare viable alternatives
      with the current direction on the factors that\nactually change the choice,
      such as timing, scope, cost, and unresolved risk.\nRecommend when to use each
      option. Do not give an unranked menu or assume that a\nfallback solves unrelated
      issues. New options proposed in this draft are not\nsaved alternatives, selected
      directions, or commitments.\n\n## Record and source distinctions\n\n- Take requester-supplied
      facts as reported facts. Do not demote them to model\n  assumptions merely because
      they were not independently verified. Flag a\n  material inconsistency when
      the records actually conflict.\n- Reconcile newer reported answers with older
      assumptions and open questions.\n  Check that material counts, dates, and totals
      agree. State the conflict and\n  its effect when they do not; do not silently
      choose a convenient value.\n  Check simple arithmetic and chronology when a
      conclusion depends on them.\n  Compare metadata with reported milestones. Put
      each material unresolved\n  inconsistency in **Record conflicts**, with the
      practical effect and the fact\n  needed to resolve it. Preserve the reported
      values; do not correct the record\n  or omit the inconsistency merely because
      the rest of the analysis can proceed.\n- Test the legal premise of an issue
      title. Name the relevant actor and explain\n  why a duty applies to that actor.
      Do not extend a rule to a different class\n  of entity without a basis, or treat
      every missing record as a breach. Where legal access to\n  sensitive records
      is restricted, distinguish permitted diligence from an\n  instruction to disclose
      or transfer the restricted material.\n- Keep model assumptions separate. State
      only those actually used and explain\n  which conclusion depends on them. Unknown
      facts remain unknown. Do not list\n  reported facts, resolved old assumptions,
      or things not assumed in this section.\n  An earlier assumption label does not
      override a later reported fact.\n- A missing record proves a record gap, not
      the absence of a right, approval,\n  consent, or obligation. Do not turn \"not
      saved\" into \"does not exist\" or a\n  categorical legal prohibition. Do not
      present an inferred business activity\n  as supplied fact. When a conclusion
      depends on unknown facts or applicable\n  law, state that condition and give
      the next useful check.\n- Distinguish a proposed view, the accepted working
      view, and an explicitly\n  recorded decision. Generating this document records
      no new decision.\n- Use the current direction's working note as fallible analysis,
      not facts.\n  Keep unresolved or stale findings qualified. Reconcile old dossier
      and research\n  assumptions against current records in the current answer; do
      not repeat a\n  superseded premise merely because preserved research still contains
      it.\n- Link support beside the claim it supports. Preserve supplied, retrieved,\n
      \ read, and verified source distinctions. Retrieval is not proof of support.\n
      \ An earlier model answer is not legal authority. Do not invent citations.\n-
      Use current support labels. Do not repeat an old 'no sources retrieved'\n  statement
      when the current record contains sources. State the actual gap.\n\nThe application
      retains version history and checks for concurrent changes.\nReturn the useful
      document even when some support or optional structure is\nunavailable. Do not
      change facts, issue status, recommendations, or decisions."
    enabled: true
    revision: e3a971907aae25fc89d3c1129bbfebf8f7fdf95b50d1b1073c18782233ac352a
    supporting_skills:
    - skill_id: answer
      path: 00_System/experimental-chat/answer.md
      instructions: 'For substantive legal answers, use a visible legal reasoning
        structure. Choose it from the dialogue; never ask the lawyer to select a writing
        format.


        Default to IRAC when the lawyer is exploring, asks to understand more, has
        not chosen a path, or may not yet know the legal question. Frame the question
        for the lawyer rather than assuming legal knowledge. Use these exact bold
        labels, each starting a separate short paragraph:


        **Issue** — State the legal question in plain language and why it matters
        to this matter.


        **Rule** — Explain the relevant rule. Link support beside the proposition
        it supports. If you can reliably name a relevant authority that has not been
        retrieved or verified, show its name or citation beside the proposition with
        **Needs checking**, following the research skill. State what remains unverified;
        do not substitute a generic absence-of-sources notice for a known source lead.


        **Analysis** — Connect the specific facts to the rule. Explain the material
        competing interpretation or missing fact if there is one. This must be reasoning,
        not a repeated rule or bare conclusion.


        **Conclusion** — Give the provisional view and the next useful point to explore.
        A recommendation is optional; understanding comes first.


        Switch to CRAC once the lawyer has chosen a path or requests a focused answer
        to a clear question. Use **Conclusion**, **Rule**, **Analysis**, and **Conclusion
        / next step**, in that order. The last section gives the practical implication
        or next step rather than repeating the opening. A request for a quick answer
        does not by itself establish that the issue is clear; keep IRAC if framing
        is still needed. If the lawyer returns to exploring or is confused, return
        to IRAC.


        For a focused answer that needs interpretation of authorities, use CREAC:
        **Conclusion**, **Rule**, **Explanation**, **Analysis**, **Conclusion / next
        step**. Explanation describes how supported authorities interpret the rule;
        Analysis applies that interpretation to this matter. Do not invent examples,
        cases, or support to fill a section.


        For a single legal question, make these reasoning labels visible. Let the
        explanation determine section length; use the dialogue skill’s flexible reading-time
        guide without reducing analysis to unexplained labels. Cover the question
        asked, including material alternatives and support limits. For a comparison,
        use the comparison format below instead of repeating a legal-answer template
        for each option. Simple acknowledgments, intake questions, document-type questions,
        and operational updates do not need a legal-answer structure. Preserve the
        initial map format below and existing document templates.


        Distinguish the model''s inference from what a source states. Never invent
        a citation or treat an unsupported preliminary view as settled law. Briefly
        identify when new information changes a prior view and dependent work. Keep
        the explanation the lawyer requested in chat. Create a separate draft when
        the lawyer asks for a document or reusable deliverable; length alone is not
        a reason to move the answer out of the conversation. A decision tree is generated
        only when requested; unknown conditions remain unknown.



        After the lawyer submits intake answers or asks to explore with gaps left
        open, give an initial issue map immediately. Keep it provisional and concise.
        Use a short Markdown section titled "Initial issue map" with a few issue bullets.
        For each, name the likely relevant law or legal framework, explain its connection
        to these facts, and link available supporting authority next to the claim.
        Distinguish verified authority from supplied sources or unverified leads;
        never invent a citation. Briefly identify unknown facts that could change
        the map. Do not treat an unsupported preliminary view as settled law.


        Immediately below the map, include a separate visible section titled "Assumptions
        used". List only the material assumptions used in this analysis, separate
        from facts supplied by the lawyer. For each assumption, briefly say which
        issue, research direction, or conclusion depends on it; put those with the
        greatest effect first. If none are needed, say "No additional assumptions
        used." Keep unknown facts unknown. Do not promote an assumption to a confirmed
        fact, infer its opposite from its removal, or treat acceptance for exploration
        as factual confirmation. Preserve hypothetical scope. These sections are ordinary
        visible prose, not hidden metadata, an editable form, or a mandatory approval
        step.


        After the initial map and assumptions, stop. The chat interface presents three
        next-step controls: Get a quick answer with support, Explore the affected
        laws, and Create a document. Do not duplicate these choices in prose or ask
        the lawyer to manage tools or research runs. Do not create clickable map items
        or assumption controls. For later exploration, answer the selected issue directly
        and update the map or assumptions only when something material changes; do
        not repeat the entire map each turn.


        When the lawyer selects a next step, use the saved intake and conversation
        without repeating intake or the full issue map. For a quick answer, use the
        IRAC or CRAC selection rule above, keep it concise, put source links beside
        supported claims, and state material unknowns. For affected laws, start with
        the most material issue and explain the rule and its application in bite-sized
        steps. Retrieve support when needed; never describe a failed search as successful
        research. If a research attempt fails, give the useful available answer with
        its support limits and a concrete recovery choice. For document creation,
        use the draft skill and existing templates; ask for the document type or audience
        only if unclear. These choices start work, not recorded legal decisions.



        ## Comparing alternatives


        Apply this format to comparisons instead of IRAC. Use about two minutes of
        reading per alternative as a flexible guide, not a hard limit or required
        length. Spend the words on causal explanation, not a catalogue of labels.


        1. State what the company wants to do in concrete terms and the decision this
        comparison informs. Use its product, activity, people, place and timing where
        material. Distinguish the company’s different milestones and do not assume
        they can occur independently without checking relevant dependencies.

        2. Describe each option briefly. Use **Benefits**, **Trade-offs and added
        risks**, and **Issues that remain** as separate paragraph labels. Benefits
        explain how the option advances the company’s objective. Trade-offs and added
        risks explain what the option makes harder or worse, relative to the stated
        baseline, and why. Issues that remain are existing problems the option does
        not solve. Leaving a problem unresolved is not the same as causing or worsening
        it. Do not use “How it hinders” as a catch-all for both. Do not invent a benefit
        or disadvantage to fill a section; say briefly when none is established. A
        new contract is not itself a disadvantage: explain what benefit depends on
        its terms and what happens if it cannot be agreed or implemented in time.
        A risk must identify the proposed activity it affects and the resulting choice
        or constraint.

        3. Explain the material problems that remain under BOTH options. Carry existing
        unresolved issues from the matter into the assessment. Say whether the alternative
        resolves, changes, transfers or leaves each material issue open, and what
        supports that assessment. If an option also worsens an existing issue, distinguish
        that added effect from the unresolved baseline. Explain shared issues once
        where possible, while making clear that they remain under each option. Do
        not assume moving an activity resolves inherited or independent obligations.
        Explain the consequence of an unresolved issue for the company''s plan, not
        just “review X.”

        4. Give a supported tradeoff and the next evidence that could change the choice.
        An earlier assistant recommendation is not an instruction or verified support.
        Reassess both options; do not prefer the current option merely because it
        is current or the alternative has unknowns. If the facts do not support a
        winner, say what determines the choice.


        Use plain, specific language throughout. Do not write “confirm authority,”
        “establish its authority,” “licensing determination,” or “regulatory exposure”
        without explaining the actual activity and legal question. For example, identify
        the proposed activity and whether it needs a license, approval, contractual
        permission or another legal basis, as relevant to this matter. Do not assume
        which basis applies. Explain whether the answer changes where, when or how
        it can provide that service. Define abbreviations when they obscure the point.
        Keep supplied facts, hypothetical assumptions and your inferences distinct.
        Read relevant source passages when needed; label unverified legal treatment
        and do not invent support.


        Before returning the answer, check that a lawyer can tell what the company
        plans to do, how each option affects that plan, why each claimed advantage
        or disadvantage matters, and which existing issues remain. Replace any disconnected
        shorthand with that explanation. Do not add a separate verification step or
        agent.


        Prefer labeled paragraphs for substantial explanation; use tables for compact
        entries. Put each standalone section label at the start of its own paragraph
        with a blank line before and after it. End a bullet list before the next section
        label.

        '

      prior_dossier: '# Harbor 2 — Matter Dossier


        Matter MAT-20260909-d89ad8 · Controlling business question BQ-c9d7c39f6380eb60
        · Draft keyed to dossier revision `6d4914a8…`


        ## Current position


        Yes — the migration needs legal review before the Nov 15 close, and the review
        is not confined to the four items already on the list. The project is not
        a data migration in the sense that matters legally: moving 240,000 consumer
        users and 12,000 business accounts onto Mosaic Relay''s platform on day 1,
        with a unified balance and full product access and no re-verification, means
        Mosaic is standing in for Harbor as the licensed and responsible institution
        for those customers from the moment of close. What changes the answer is that
        one of the plan''s headline benefits is also its weakest legal link: the "44-state
        combined footprint" is only an advantage if Mosaic can actually serve the
        customers in the states where it holds no license of its own, and the reported
        deal structure is an asset purchase, which is the structure least likely to
        carry Harbor''s money transmitter licenses (MTLs) across.


        The recommended course is to keep Nov 15 as the close target but decouple
        it from a full-scope day-1 migration. Close can proceed; the "one unified
        account, full access, 44 states" launch should be treated as a separate, staged
        plan whose scope is set by three answers that are obtainable now: whether
        the purchased assets include the equity of Harbor''s licensed entities, whether
        the pre-2023 KYC records can be recovered, and what the unreviewed alerts
        and SARs show.


        What can proceed while those answers are obtained: the deal mechanics, the
        migration build and test loads for the states where Mosaic holds its own license,
        and the customer-communication design. What should wait or change: activating
        customers in the states where only Harbor is licensed; activating pre-2023
        users who have no underlying verification documents without either recovered
        records or a re-verification step; launching the $50 welcome bonus on close+1
        before its terms are reviewed; and cutting over transaction monitoring without
        a validated no-gap plan.


        The decisive conditions, in order of how much they change the plan: (1) whether
        the licensed Harbor entities are inside or outside the purchased assets —
        this determines whether the four-state piece is a filing exercise or a service-scope
        cut; (2) whether the pre-2023 identity records exist somewhere recoverable
        — this determines how many of the 240,000 users can be activated on day 1
        without re-verification; (3) whether the alert/SAR review reveals unremediated
        suspicious activity touching the migrating book — this affects both the deal
        terms and whether specific accounts should migrate at all; (4) whether Harbor''s
        monitoring vendor contract can be extended or bridged — this determines whether
        there is a control gap at the worst possible moment.


        Where this stands: the records read contain no formally adopted working view
        and no recorded decision beyond the intake answers themselves. The intake
        answers are reported facts (structure = asset purchase; plan = use/assume
        Harbor''s licenses; alerts and SARs unreviewed; KYC reliance question outstanding
        with compliance). The earlier assistant analyses proposed treating legal and
        compliance readiness as a pre-close gate and ranked the unreviewed alerts
        and SARs as the highest risk; that is fallible prior analysis, not authority
        and not an adopted decision. The staging recommendation above is this draft''s,
        and generating this document records no decision.


        ## Decision question


        Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before
        the Nov 15 close?


        ## Issues


        The captured records contain a saved issue list, but its stable IDs were not
        retrievable within this run''s reading allowance, so the issues below use
        ordinary headings and carry no `ISS-` markers. Items 1–5 are the issues carried
        in the matter''s intake record and earlier analyses; item 6 is identified
        in this draft from the same reported facts.


        ### 1. Serving the new states under Harbor''s licenses (reported asset purchase)


        **Current answer**


        Under the reported structure — Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets — Mosaic most
        likely cannot "use/assume" Harbor''s MTLs for the states where Mosaic holds
        no license of its own. A money transmitter license is issued to a specific
        licensed entity and, on the general rule, does not travel with the purchase
        of assets; the license stays with Harbor''s entity while the assets move.
        If that is the structure, the states where only Harbor is licensed cannot
        be served by Mosaic at close, and new state applications run on a scale of
        months, not the roughly ten weeks to Nov 15. The practical answer is that
        this part of the day-1 plan should be cut or phased, not reviewed and cleared.
        The operating exception, which is the single most important thing to check,
        is whether the deal in fact takes the licensed entity (equity) as well as
        the assets — see Record conflicts.


        **Rule and support**


        State money transmission licensing regimes, administered by state banking
        or financial-institutions departments, grant authority to a named licensee
        and condition any change of control, merger, or acquisition of the licensed
        entity on notice or prior approval. The proposition that licenses generally
        do not transfer with an asset sale, and the exact filing route and timing
        in each relevant state, are unverified: no authority was retrieved in this
        run and none appears in the portions of the record read. Named leads requiring
        checking: state money transmitter licensing statutes and their change-of-control
        provisions; the Money Transmission Modernization Act, which several states
        have adopted and which standardizes how acquisitions and license transfers
        are handled — **Needs checking**. Support in the record: the reported structure,
        asset purchase, answered 2026-09-09 ([source:FACT-20260909-ed9f06]); the plan
        to use or assume Harbor''s licenses ([source:FACT-20260909-f0fb01], [source:FACT-20260909-771ee1]);
        the license counts ([source:FACT-20260909-33293c]).


        **Application**


        The decisive term is whether the purchased assets include the equity of Harbor''s
        licensed entity. If the deal buys the entity, the question becomes change-of-control
        approvals and notices in each state — those are not automatic at close either,
        and if no filings were started months ago they will not land by Nov 15; Harbor''s
        existing licenses may continue to cover accounts served by Harbor''s entity
        in the interim, which is a different launch structure (Harbor-branded or Harbor-entity
        servicing). If the deal buys assets only, Mosaic needs its own license in
        each of the states where it does not have one, and no amount of diligence
        compresses that timeline. Either way, the day-1 promise of full product access
        across the combined footprint is the part that must give; customers in the
        states where Mosaic already holds its own license are not affected by this
        issue. The number of states in play is itself unsettled: the reported figures
        imply three Harbor-only states, not four (Record conflicts). The other material
        condition is what "full access to our product set" means for customers in
        the non-overlapping states — if Mosaic''s licensed entity can serve some products
        but not others, the cut is by product line rather than by state, and that
        mapping should be part of this review rather than assumed by the integration
        team.


        **Next step**


        Obtain the purchase agreement''s asset schedule and a written answer on whether
        Harbor''s licensed entities (and their licenses) are inside or outside the
        purchased assets. In parallel, have state licensing counsel produce a table
        of every state where Mosaic does not hold its own license, with the required
        filing, its realistic timeline, and whether any temporary authority to operate
        pending approval exists. That table becomes the day-1 launch map. If the answer
        is assets-only, treat the non-overlapping states as post-close expansion.


        ### 2. KYC/CIP: relying on Harbor''s prior verification and the pre-2023 records
        gap


        **Current answer**


        The "no re-verification" plan is unproven on two separate points, and the
        second one is unlikely to be curable by policy. First, whether Mosaic''s own
        AML/CIP program permits reliance on another institution''s prior verification
        is still open with compliance — recorded on 2026-09-09 as "not sure / need
        to check." Second, and more concretely, reliance on another institution''s
        verification ordinarily presupposes that the other institution''s records
        can be obtained; for Harbor users onboarded before 2023 the underlying documents
        are gone because the vendor that ran the checks shut down in 2024. A pass/fail
        flag without the identifying information and the verification description
        is a weak foundation for recordkeeping obligations that run to the identity
        of the customer. The working answer is that the pre-2023 cohort should be
        planned as requiring either recovered records or a re-verification step before
        the accounts get full functionality; the 2023-and-later cohort may be capable
        of being relied upon if the records survived and Mosaic''s program allows
        it. Whether Mosaic — a money transmitter — can use the reliance provision
        at all depends on its scope, which is a legal question, not only a compliance-policy
        question, and it belongs in the written answer.


        **Rule and support**


        The Bank Secrecy Act and FinCEN''s implementing rules require a money services
        business to maintain a written anti-money laundering program and to identify
        and verify customers and retain records of the information relied upon. The
        customer identification program rules applicable to money services businesses
        (31 C.F.R. Part 1022) and the reliance provision that lets an institution
        lean on another institution''s performance of those elements are **Needs checking**
        — the reliance provision has conditions (including that the other institution
        be subject to an AML program requirement and that the relying institution
        obtain the records within a reasonable time) that decide this issue, and none
        of that was retrieved. Entity customers among the 12,000 business accounts
        raise separate due-diligence questions, and whether Mosaic must collect beneficial-ownership
        information for Harbor''s business customers depends on which CDD rules apply
        to its business — **Needs checking**. Support in the record: no re-verification
        plan ([source:FACT-20260909-9a0c61], [source:FACT-20260909-f2c49f]); vendor
        shutdown and pre-2023 document gap ([source:FACT-20260909-aea8ec], [source:FACT-20260909-13d4c1]);
        compliance confirmation outstanding ([source:FACT-20260909-b5e71e], [source:FACT-20260909-620c62]).


        **Application**


        Break the 252,000 migrated accounts into three populations and treat each
        differently. Consumers onboarded in 2023 or later, with verification records
        retained: reliance analysis governs, and the answer turns on Mosaic''s program
        language and on whether the records can be produced on request. Consumers
        onboarded before 2023 with no underlying documents: no policy permission cures
        a missing record, so the real options are recovery, re-verification, or restricted
        functionality. Recovery is worth a genuine attempt rather than an assumption
        — when a KYC vendor shuts down, its records are sometimes held by a successor,
        a receiver, or an escrow agent, and Harbor may also hold images or copies
        outside the vendor''s system. The 12,000 business accounts need separate treatment:
        entity customers generally require more information than a pass/fail flag,
        their files are harder to re-verify at scale, and they are the accounts most
        likely to need beneficial-ownership data. The decisive fact for how many users
        can be activated on day 1 is the split between the cohorts and whether any
        recovery is possible; without that, the migration plan should carry a re-verification
        path rather than assume zero.


        **Next step**


        Get compliance''s written answer to the question already recorded — whether
        the program permits reliance and on what conditions — together with counts
        for the pre-2023 cohort across consumer and business accounts, and a records-recovery
        attempt against Harbor, the vendor''s successor, and any escrow. The deliverable
        is a cohort-by-cohort onboarding plan with a projected day-1 activation number.
        Fallback if records are unrecoverable and reliance is unavailable: re-verify
        the pre-2023 cohort at first login and hold full functionality until verification
        completes.


        ### 3. The unreviewed open alerts and SAR history


        **Current answer**


        Nothing has been reviewed, so the honest current answer is that no one can
        yet say whether the acquired book carries ordinary-course monitoring noise
        or unremediated suspicious activity touching specific customers who are about
        to be onboarded to Mosaic. This is the item most capable of changing the deal
        — price, indemnity, or a closing condition — and it also constrains the migration,
        because it determines whether particular accounts should be excluded from
        automatic day-1 migration or activated under conditions. There is also a procedural
        constraint the plan does not appear to have accounted for: suspicious activity
        reports carry confidentiality restrictions, so this review has to run under
        a controlled protocol rather than by handing Harbor''s alert and SAR files
        to the deal team.


        **Rule and support**


        The Bank Secrecy Act''s suspicious activity reporting and confidentiality
        provisions, 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g), and the SAR rules applicable to money services
        businesses, 31 C.F.R. § 1022.320, impose filing obligations and restrict disclosure
        of a SAR''s existence, with a defined framework for lawful sharing — **Needs
        checking**; no authority was retrieved in this run, and the precise sharing
        route (including through counsel and any permitted disclosure to a counterparty)
        is the legal question to answer before the files move anywhere. Support in
        the record: ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from the last year, none
        read ([source:FACT-20260909-adf2cb], [source:FACT-20260909-9f7bde]); confirmation
        that review is still in diligence ([source:FACT-20260909-849b00], [source:FACT-20260909-070aec]).


        **Application**


        Two outputs should come out of the same review, and they should not be mixed.
        For the deal: whether anything in the file requires disclosure, repricing,
        a specific indemnity, or a pre-closing remediation condition, and whether
        any of it implicates Harbor''s program adequacy rather than isolated customer
        conduct. For the migration: whether any account in the 252,000 is connected
        to an unresolved alert or an unreported pattern, and if so whether it should
        be excluded, migrated with monitoring, or held for review — an account-level
        answer, not a population-level one. The record gives "~40" and "a handful,"
        neither of which is a count; the size of the SAR file itself is unknown, and
        until the review runs, the practical effect is that the deal team cannot represent
        to itself, or to a regulator later, what it acquired. Timing matters more
        than completeness: a review of the alerts plus a readout on the SARs is achievable
        pre-close if it starts now, and it is the difference between a known and an
        unknown liability.


        **Next step**


        Set up a counsel-led, need-to-know review with a documented protocol for handling
        SAR material (proposed owner: outside AML/BSA counsel together with Mosaic''s
        BSA officer, starting immediately, with the readout before the purchase agreement
        is finalized). Deliverable: an inventory plus a written readout separated
        into deal items and migration items. Fallback if the review cannot complete
        pre-close: make it an express condition or hold completion/indemnity for its
        outcome rather than letting the gap close quietly.


        ### 4. Transaction monitoring cutover


        **Current answer**


        Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party service whose contract terminates at
        close, and the plan is to point Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s engine
        on day 1. As a legal matter the item needs review because transaction monitoring
        is a required element of the AML program, and the records show no evidence
        of a tested transition: no rule mapping, no parallel-run decision, no cutover
        criteria, and no owner. The gap exposure is precise — Harbor''s vendor stops
        covering the book at the same moment the largest customer event in the matter
        occurs — and it should be closed commercially as well as technically, which
        means deciding now whether to extend the vendor contract for a transition
        period.


        **Rule and support**


        Money services businesses must maintain a risk-based AML program that includes
        monitoring and reporting of suspicious activity; the program elements and
        the expectation that changes to them be documented and validated are **Needs
        checking** (the monitoring-specific requirements were not retrieved). Support
        in the record: the SaaS contract terminates at close with a day-1 repoint
        plan ([source:FACT-20260909-073838], [source:FACT-20260909-78d5cd]); the unread
        alert inventory, which is the evidence that monitoring at Harbor was already
        behind ([source:FACT-20260909-9f7bde]).


        **Application**


        The decisive unknowns are the vendor contract''s actual end date relative
        to close, whether it can be extended and on what notice, what happens to alerts
        the vendor would have generated during any gap, and whether Mosaic''s engine''s
        scenarios were tuned for this book (new products, higher transaction velocity,
        business accounts, multi-state activity). If coverage ends at close and Mosaic''s
        engine is not validated by then, the migrated accounts pass through a window
        with no effective monitoring — and the alert review in Issue 3 will not be
        representative of that window. Mitigation is either parallel running (both
        engines for a defined period) or a short vendor extension; both require a
        decision now because they depend on the vendor''s agreement and on a test
        period. Legal review''s function here is not to bless the integration but
        to make the transition documentable: who monitors what during the window,
        who files what if something surfaces, and what evidence exists that the change
        was controlled.


        **Next step**


        Confirm the contract end date and extension terms with the vendor, and produce
        a cutover plan with test scenarios, pass criteria, an accountable owner, and
        an explicit parallel-run or extension decision (proposed owner: integration/operations
        lead with the BSA officer; before the agreement is signed, because the extension
        is a commercial commitment). Fallback if no extension is available: run Mosaic''s
        engine in parallel ahead of the lapse and impose temporary limits on high-risk
        activity types until validation passes.


        ### 5. The $50 welcome bonus campaign


        **Current answer**


        The campaign launches close+1 and no terms are in the records, so what is
        needed is a short, concrete review rather than a legal question: the offer''s
        eligibility and payment mechanics, its abuse controls, and the advertising
        content in the states where it will run. The specific risk worth attention
        is that "a $50 bonus on first transfer" can be drafted in a way that pays
        users for moving money through the app, which is both a disclosure problem
        and a fraud/loss problem. The second issue is footprint: the bonus should
        not run in states where Mosaic cannot yet lawfully serve the customers, so
        its state list should be the migration''s approved state list.


        **Rule and support**


        State consumer protection and unfair-or-deceptive-practices statutes and state-specific
        promotion rules can attach to advertised cash incentives, and money transmitter
        marketing can carry additional disclosure requirements; the specific authorities
        were not retrieved — **Needs checking**. The terms checklist itself (eligibility,
        funding vs. transfer trigger, payment mechanics and timing, expiry, per-user
        limits, claw-back, tax treatment) comes from the earlier analysis in this
        matter, not from retrieved authority. Support in the record: the campaign,
        the $50 amount, and the close+1 launch ([source:FACT-20260909-19aebc]).


        **Application**


        The term that changes the answer is what counts as a "first transfer": if
        it includes a user moving money between their own accounts or a manufactured
        transfer, the promotion creates an incentive for exactly the activity the
        monitoring program is supposed to catch, and the abuse controls need to be
        written into the terms, not bolted on later. Eligibility also needs to state
        whether migrated Harbor users qualify — that is a business choice, but it
        determines the campaign''s cost and its state footprint, and it interacts
        with the pre-2023 cohort if those users are not fully activated on day 1.
        The tax question (whether $50 payments are reportable, and to whom) is a tax-team
        item that should be routed in parallel rather than answered here.


        **Next step**


        Obtain the campaign terms and the intended state list and route them through
        a short review against the checklist above (proposed owner: marketing counsel
        with compliance). Deliverable: a marked-up terms sheet plus a one-page approval.
        Fallback if the terms are not ready: move the launch date; close+1 is a business
        choice, while having documented terms before advertising is not.


        ### 6. Transfer of customer contracts, balances, and customer data (identified
        in this draft)


        **Current answer**


        An asset purchase does not by itself move customer relationships, balances,
        or personal data to the buyer. The record does not say whether Harbor''s customer
        agreements are being assigned, whether they permit assignment without consent,
        or what notice customers are entitled to before their accounts and balances
        appear inside Mosaic''s app. This matters to the business question directly:
        if the agreements require notice or consent, day 1 is not a silent system
        migration but a customer-facing event with a timeline, and the activation
        count changes. This issue is separate from licensing and AML — fixing those
        does not fix this — and it applies to both the 240,000 consumer accounts and
        the 12,000 business accounts, whose agreements may contain negotiated assignment
        terms.


        **Rule and support**


        Contract assignment and novation analysis on Harbor''s consumer and business
        customer agreements (whether assignment is permitted, permitted on notice,
        or requires consent, and what happens to balances if it is neither); and the
        privacy and data-transfer regime applicable to moving consumer financial data
        — the Gramm-Leach-Bliley privacy and data-safeguards framework, for which
        the FTC rules at 16 C.F.R. Parts 313 and 314 are the usual lead for a non-bank
        money transmitter — **Needs checking**; nothing was retrieved in this run
        and the agreements are not in the portions of the record read. Support in
        the record: asset purchase structure ([source:FACT-20260909-ed9f06]); day-1
        move of 240,000 consumer users and 12,000 business accounts into one unified
        account and balance with full product access ([source:FACT-20260909-551367],
        [source:FACT-20260909-4c1fd8]).


        **Application**


        "One unified account, one balance" means Mosaic is not merely hosting data
        from day 1; it is standing in for Harbor as custodian of those balances. The
        term that decides this issue is the assignment clause in the customer agreements
        and the corresponding provision in the purchase agreement: if the agreements
        assign freely, day 1 can be a notice event; if they require consent or allow
        objection, day 1 becomes a notice-and-objection process, which changes the
        migration calendar and probably the activation count. A second question sits
        alongside it: "full access to our product set" may add products the existing
        customer agreements do not contemplate, which is a contract-scope question
        independent of whether the account itself could be transferred.


        **Next step**


        Pull the asset schedule and a representative sample of the consumer and business
        customer agreements, and get a written answer on assignment and noticeability,
        mapped against the migration timeline (proposed owner: commercial contracts
        counsel, starting immediately so the notice path can be designed in parallel
        with the migration build). Fallback if assignments are not clean: run day
        1 as a continuation of the existing accounts with a customer notice campaign
        and a later conversion, rather than an instantaneous transfer of balances.

        ## Record conflicts


        The state counts do not produce the stated number of new markets. Reported:
        Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, Mosaic in 41, combined footprint 44, "opens
        four new markets." The arithmetic gives 38 + 41 − 44 = 35 states held by both,
        so Harbor-only states = 3 and Mosaic-only states = 6. Mosaic gains three states
        from the combination, not four, unless "markets" is defined differently (for
        example counting a district or territory, or counting markets where Harbor''s
        license covers a product Mosaic cannot offer, or a counting error). Practical
        effect: the number of jurisdictions requiring a new license, notice, or approval
        — and therefore the day-1 scope and the filing workload before Nov 15 — is
        uncertain by one state. Resolve with the licensing team''s actual state list.
        Note also that the two facts rows do not conflict with each other; the discrepancy
        is internal to the 38/41/44/4 figures.


        The recorded plan to use Harbor''s licenses sits against the recorded structure.
        The intake answer says Mosaic plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for
        the new markets ([source:FACT-20260909-f0fb01], [source:FACT-20260909-771ee1]),
        while the structure is an asset purchase ([source:FACT-20260909-ed9f06]).
        Those two answers cannot both be acted on without qualification. Practical
        effect: if the licensed entity is not part of the purchase, the plan is not
        available and the four-state launch must be cut or phased. Resolve with the
        asset schedule (Next action 1).


        Matter metadata records a target date that does not match the reported close.
        The matter record shows `target_date: 2026-09-11`, two days after the original
        request, while the reported close is Nov 15. The records read do not explain
        what 2026-09-11 measures (a work target, a next-touch date, or something else).
        Practical effect: if 2026-09-11 is a real internal milestone, the ranked actions
        above need compressing into that window; if it is not, the Nov 15 close governs.
        Resolve by confirming what the field represents.


        ## Assumptions used


        For the licensing analysis I assume the asset purchase does not include the
        equity of Harbor''s licensed entities, because that is the most natural reading
        of the reported answer "asset purchase (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)." If
        the licensed entity transfers, Issue 1 changes from "obtain licenses" to "change-of-control
        approvals," which changes the timing and the available interim structure but
        may not remove the pre-close constraint. Issue 1''s current answer, the day-1
        footprint recommendation, and Next actions 1 and 2 depend on this.


        I assume the migration plan means Harbor''s customers can transact in all
        covered states immediately at close, because the request describes one unified
        account, one balance, and full access on day 1. If the plan in fact holds
        back the non-overlapping states until licenses or approvals are in place,
        Issue 1 becomes a phasing question rather than a pre-close blocker, and the
        urgency of Next actions 1 and 2 drops. The Current position staging recommendation
        depends on this.


        I assume the "no re-verification" plan applies to the 12,000 business accounts
        as well as the 240,000 consumer accounts, since the request describes a single
        migration with no re-verification. If business accounts are handled under
        a separate process, the entity-customer portion of Issue 2 narrows, though
        the pre-2023 problem does not. Issue 2''s application and Next action 3 depend
        on this.


        I carry forward the saved assumption, not yet confirmed, that Harbor Pay is
        a licensed money transmitter subject to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML
        obligations, and that Mosaic Relay holds 41 state licenses as reported. If
        Harbor''s licensing status differs, the framing of Issues 1 and 3 changes.
        Those issues depend on it.


        Not listed: the earlier saved assumption that the acquisition structure was
        unconfirmed; that has been superseded by the reported asset purchase answer
        of 2026-09-09, and the licensing analysis treats the structure as reported
        rather than assumed.

        ```text
        # Original Request


        From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

        Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


        We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
        plan:


        240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
        One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

        No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

        Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
        opens four new markets.

        Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
        results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded
        before 2023.

        Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
        Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

        Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
        close+1.

        Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs
        from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


        Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.

        # Company profile


        ## Company Name


        Mosaic Relay


        ## Website Url


        Not provided.


        ## Summary


        Mosaic Relay is a fictional payment infrastructure company created only for
        this Counsel OS UX experiment. It has no real-company affiliation and must
        not be confused with Stripe, Checkout.com, Marqeta, Manifest Financial, Chime,
        or any other real company. Business model: Mosaic Relay sells API and hosted
        infrastructure to online businesses, marketplaces, and software platforms.
        It charges platform and usage fees for payment acceptance, risk, operations,
        and payout tools. It is not a bank. It does not offer bank accounts, hold
        deposits, take deposits, or operate as a bank. Products and services: APIs
        and hosted tools for card, ACH, and local payment acceptance; payment routing
        and splits; refunds and disputes; seller, contractor, and recipient payouts;
        merchant onboarding; identity verification; KYB and KYC; sanctions screening;
        fraud monitoring; transaction risk scoring; payout controls; reconciliation;
        and operations dashboards. Customers: online businesses, marketplaces, and
        software platforms, including businesses that onboard sellers, contractors,
        or recipients. Mosaic Relay supports their payment operations but does not
        take custody of customer deposits. Partners and dependencies: acquiring banks,
        payment processors, card networks, identity and fraud vendors, and cloud providers.
        These are third-party relationships, not ownership or affiliation. Footprint
        and teams: fictional US-headquartered company serving customers in North America,
        the UK, EU, and selected other markets through remote and regional teams.
        Core teams are product and engineering, payments operations, risk and trust,
        compliance and financial crime, sales and customer success, security and privacy,
        finance, and legal. Legal topics: BSA/AML and financial-crime controls; money
        transmission and payments regulation; card-network and processor rules; ACH
        and local-payment rules; consumer protection and funds-flow disclosures; privacy
        and data protection; cybersecurity and incident response; sanctions; KYB/KYC
        and identity; vendor and cloud contracts; commercial terms; IP; employment;
        and marketing compliance. Risk posture: moderate-to-high regulatory and operational
        risk because the platform supports payment acceptance, onboarding, risk decisions,
        and payouts. Mosaic Relay uses risk-based controls, clear ownership, documented
        escalation, auditability, vendor oversight, data minimization, and human review
        for material exceptions. It aims to prevent fraud, sanctions breaches, unsafe
        payouts, and misleading customer claims while keeping the product usable.
        Operating principles: be accurate about what Mosaic Relay does and does not
        do; separate recommendations from recorded decisions; state material assumptions;
        preserve an editable work product; avoid claiming licenses, registrations,
        approvals, or bank status unless confirmed; protect personal data; and favor
        a useful first pass with clear gaps over a blank result. Fictional legal owner:
        Jordan Lee, fictional General Counsel and Head of Regulatory Affairs for Mosaic
        Relay. Jordan owns legal decisions and escalation. The company, people, partners,
        customers, and footprint described here are fictional for testing.


        ## Business Model


        Sells API and hosted infrastructure to online businesses, marketplaces, and
        software platforms. Charges platform and usage fees for payment acceptance,
        risk, operations, and payout tools. Not a bank; does not hold or take deposits.

        APIs and hosted tools for card, ACH, and local payment acceptance; payment

        payouts; merchant onboarding; identity verification; KYB and KYC; sanctions
        screening; fraud monitoring; transaction risk scoring; payout controls; reconciliation;
        and operations dashboards.


        ## Jurisdictions


        US-headquartered; serves customers in North America, the UK, EU, and selected
        other markets through remote and regional teams.


        ## Regulatory Context


        Subject to BSA/AML and financial-crime controls; money transmission and payments
        regulation; card-network and processor rules; ACH and local-payment rules;
        consumer protection and funds-flow disclosures; privacy and data protection;
        cybersecurity and incident response; sanctions; KYB/KYC and identity; vendor
        and cloud contracts; commercial terms; IP; employment; and marketing compliance.


        ## Data Practices


        Processes personal data in connection with identity verification, KYB/KYC,

        ## Risk Posture


        Moderate-to-high regulatory and operational risk due to payment acceptance,

        documented escalation, auditability, vendor oversight, data minimization,
        and human review for material exceptions. Aims to prevent fraud, sanctions
        breaches, unsafe payouts, and misleading customer claims while keeping the
        product usable.

        # source_file: FILE-1e32b92b3dce3fe1c8cb6f2a

        # Harbor 2 — Matter Dossier


        Matter MAT-20260909-d89ad8 · Controlling business question BQ-c9d7c39f6380eb60
        · Draft keyed to dossier revision `6d4914a8…`


        ## Current position


        Yes — the migration needs legal review before the Nov 15 close, and the review
        is not confined to the four items already on the list. The project is not
        a data migration in the sense that matters legally: moving 240,000 consumer
        users and 12,000 business accounts onto Mosaic Relay''s platform on day 1,
        with a unified balance and full product access and no re-verification, means
        Mosaic is standing in for Harbor as the licensed and responsible institution
        for those customers from the moment of close. What changes the answer is that
        one of the plan''s headline benefits is also its weakest legal link: the "44-state
        combined footprint" is only an advantage if Mosaic can actually serve the
        customers in the states where it holds no license of its own, and the reported
        deal structure is an asset purchase, which is the structure least likely to
        carry Harbor''s money transmitter licenses (MTLs) across.


        The recommended course is to keep Nov 15 as the close target but decouple
        it from a full-scope day-1 migration. Close can proceed; the "one unified
        account, full access, 44 states" launch should be treated as a separate, staged
        plan whose scope is set by three answers that are obtainable now: whether
        the purchased assets include the equity of Harbor''s licensed entities, whether
        the pre-2023 KYC records can be recovered, and what the unreviewed alerts
        and SARs show.


        What can proceed while those answers are obtained: the deal mechanics, the
        migration build and test loads for the states where Mosaic holds its own license,
        and the customer-communication design. What should wait or change: activating
        customers in the states where only Harbor is licensed; activating pre-2023
        users who have no underlying verification documents without either recovered
        records or a re-verification step; launching the $50 welcome bonus on close+1
        before its terms are reviewed; and cutting over transaction monitoring without
        a validated no-gap plan.


        The decisive conditions, in order of how much they change the plan: (1) whether
        the licensed Harbor entities are inside or outside the purchased assets —
        this determines whether the four-state piece is a filing exercise or a service-scope
        cut; (2) whether the pre-2023 identity records exist somewhere recoverable
        — this determines how many of the 240,000 users can be activated on day 1
        without re-verification; (3) whether the alert/SAR review reveals unremediated
        suspicious activity touching the migrating book — this affects both the deal
        terms and whether specific accounts should migrate at all; (4) whether Harbor''s
        monitoring vendor contract can be extended or bridged — this determines whether
        there is a control gap at the worst possible moment.


        Where this stands: the records read contain no formally adopted working view
        and no recorded decision beyond the intake answers themselves. The intake
        answers are reported facts (structure = asset purchase; plan = use/assume
        Harbor''s licenses; alerts and SARs unreviewed; KYC reliance question outstanding
        with compliance). The earlier assistant analyses proposed treating legal and
        compliance readiness as a pre-close gate and ranked the unreviewed alerts
        and SARs as the highest risk; that is fallible prior analysis, not authority
        and not an adopted decision. The staging recommendation above is this draft''s,
        and generating this document records no decision.


        ## Decision question


        Does any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration need legal review before
        the Nov 15 close?


        ## Issues


        The captured records contain a saved issue list, but its stable IDs were not
        retrievable within this run''s reading allowance, so the issues below use
        ordinary headings and carry no `ISS-` markers. Items 1–5 are the issues carried
        in the matter''s intake record and earlier analyses; item 6 is identified
        in this draft from the same reported facts.


        ### 1. Serving the new states under Harbor''s licenses (reported asset purchase)


        **Current answer**


        Under the reported structure — Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets — Mosaic most
        likely cannot "use/assume" Harbor''s MTLs for the states where Mosaic holds
        no license of its own. A money transmitter license is issued to a specific
        licensed entity and, on the general rule, does not travel with the purchase
        of assets; the license stays with Harbor''s entity while the assets move.
        If that is the structure, the states where only Harbor is licensed cannot
        be served by Mosaic at close, and new state applications run on a scale of
        months, not the roughly ten weeks to Nov 15. The practical answer is that
        this part of the day-1 plan should be cut or phased, not reviewed and cleared.
        The operating exception, which is the single most important thing to check,
        is whether the deal in fact takes the licensed entity (equity) as well as
        the assets — see Record conflicts.


        **Rule and support**


        State money transmission licensing regimes, administered by state banking
        or financial-institutions departments, grant authority to a named licensee
        and condition any change of control, merger, or acquisition of the licensed
        entity on notice or prior approval. The proposition that licenses generally
        do not transfer with an asset sale, and the exact filing route and timing
        in each relevant state, are unverified: no authority was retrieved in this
        run and none appears in the portions of the record read. Named leads requiring
        checking: state money transmitter licensing statutes and their change-of-control
        provisions; the Money Transmission Modernization Act, which several states
        have adopted and which standardizes how acquisitions and license transfers
        are handled — **Needs checking**. Support in the record: the reported structure,
        asset purchase, answered 2026-09-09 ([source:FACT-20260909-ed9f06]); the plan
        to use or assume Harbor''s licenses ([source:FACT-20260909-f0fb01], [source:FACT-20260909-771ee1]);
        the license counts ([source:FACT-20260909-33293c]).


        **Application**


        The decisive term is whether the purchased assets include the equity of Harbor''s
        licensed entity. If the deal buys the entity, the question becomes change-of-control
        approvals and notices in each state — those are not automatic at close either,
        and if no filings were started months ago they will not land by Nov 15; Harbor''s
        existing licenses may continue to cover accounts served by Harbor''s entity
        in the interim, which is a different launch structure (Harbor-branded or Harbor-entity
        servicing). If the deal buys assets only, Mosaic needs its own license in
        each of the states where it does not have one, and no amount of diligence
        compresses that timeline. Either way, the day-1 promise of full product access
        across the combined footprint is the part that must give; customers in the
        states where Mosaic already holds its own license are not affected by this
        issue. The number of states in play is itself unsettled: the reported figures
        imply three Harbor-only states, not four (Record conflicts). The other material
        condition is what "full access to our product set" means for customers in
        the non-overlapping states — if Mosaic''s licensed entity can serve some products
        but not others, the cut is by product line rather than by state, and that
        mapping should be part of this review rather than assumed by the integration
        team.


        **Next step**


        Obtain the purchase agreement''s asset schedule and a written answer on whether
        Harbor''s licensed entities (and their licenses) are inside or outside the
        purchased assets. In parallel, have state licensing counsel produce a table
        of every state where Mosaic does not hold its own license, with the required
        filing, its realistic timeline, and whether any temporary authority to operate
        pending approval exists. That table becomes the day-1 launch map. If the answer
        is assets-only, treat the non-overlapping states as post-close expansion.


        ### 2. KYC/CIP: relying on Harbor''s prior verification and the pre-2023 records
        gap


        **Current answer**


        The "no re-verification" plan is unproven on two separate points, and the
        second one is unlikely to be curable by policy. First, whether Mosaic''s own
        AML/CIP program permits reliance on another institution''s prior verification
        is still open with compliance — recorded on 2026-09-09 as "not sure / need
        to check." Second, and more concretely, reliance on another institution''s
        verification ordinarily presupposes that the other institution''s records
        can be obtained; for Harbor users onboarded before 2023 the underlying documents
        are gone because the vendor that ran the checks shut down in 2024. A pass/fail
        flag without the identifying information and the verification description
        is a weak foundation for recordkeeping obligations that run to the identity
        of the customer. The working answer is that the pre-2023 cohort should be
        planned as requiring either recovered records or a re-verification step before
        the accounts get full functionality; the 2023-and-later cohort may be capable
        of being relied upon if the records survived and Mosaic''s program allows
        it. Whether Mosaic — a money transmitter — can use the reliance provision
        at all depends on its scope, which is a legal question, not only a compliance-policy
        question, and it belongs in the written answer.


        **Rule and support**


        The Bank Secrecy Act and FinCEN''s implementing rules require a money services
        business to maintain a written anti-money laundering program and to identify
        and verify customers and retain records of the information relied upon. The
        customer identification program rules applicable to money services businesses
        (31 C.F.R. Part 1022) and the reliance provision that lets an institution
        lean on another institution''s performance of those elements are **Needs checking**
        — the reliance provision has conditions (including that the other institution
        be subject to an AML program requirement and that the relying institution
        obtain the records within a reasonable time) that decide this issue, and none
        of that was retrieved. Entity customers among the 12,000 business accounts
        raise separate due-diligence questions, and whether Mosaic must collect beneficial-ownership
        information for Harbor''s business customers depends on which CDD rules apply
        to its business — **Needs checking**. Support in the record: no re-verification
        plan ([source:FACT-20260909-9a0c61], [source:FACT-20260909-f2c49f]); vendor
        shutdown and pre-2023 document gap ([source:FACT-20260909-aea8ec], [source:FACT-20260909-13d4c1]);
        compliance confirmation outstanding ([source:FACT-20260909-b5e71e], [source:FACT-20260909-620c62]).


        **Application**


        Break the 252,000 migrated accounts into three populations and treat each
        differently. Consumers onboarded in 2023 or later, with verification records
        retained: reliance analysis governs, and the answer turns on Mosaic''s program
        language and on whether the records can be produced on request. Consumers
        onboarded before 2023 with no underlying documents: no policy permission cures
        a missing record, so the real options are recovery, re-verification, or restricted
        functionality. Recovery is worth a genuine attempt rather than an assumption
        — when a KYC vendor shuts down, its records are sometimes held by a successor,
        a receiver, or an escrow agent, and Harbor may also hold images or copies
        outside the vendor''s system. The 12,000 business accounts need separate treatment:
        entity customers generally require more information than a pass/fail flag,
        their files are harder to re-verify at scale, and they are the accounts most
        likely to need beneficial-ownership data. The decisive fact for how many users
        can be activated on day 1 is the split between the cohorts and whether any
        recovery is possible; without that, the migration plan should carry a re-verification
        path rather than assume zero.


        **Next step**

        ```

      - message_id: MSG-20260909-982278
        role: user
        content: 'From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

          Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


          We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
          plan:


          240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
          One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

          No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

          Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
          opens four new markets.

          Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
          results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded
          before 2023.

          Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at
          close. Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

          Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer,
          launching close+1.

          Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs
          from the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


          Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.'

      - message_id: MSG-20260909-7825a0
        role: assistant
        content: 'I''ve recorded the intake. Here''s my orientation to the request.


          **Summary of the request:** Dana (PM, Growth & Integration) asks whether
          the Harbor Pay acquisition migration needs legal review before the Nov 15
          close (~10 weeks out). The plan moves 240k consumer users and 12k business
          accounts into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1, with no re-verification of Harbor''s
          KYC, repointing Harbor''s monitoring feed to Mosaic''s engine, a $50 welcome
          bonus, and unread open alerts/SARs. Dana frames it as "really just a data
          migration."


          **My read:** This is not just a data migration. It raises at least five
          legal workstreams that need attention before close:


          - **Money transmission licensing** — the combined 44-state footprint and
          whether Harbor''s MTLs transfer or must be re-applied for in the four new
          markets.

          - **BSA/AML and KYC** — whether Mosaic can rely on Harbor''s prior KYC without
          re-verification, especially where pre-2023 underlying documents are missing.

          - **SARs and open alerts** — ~40 open alerts and a handful of SARs carry
          potential unresolved BSA/AML obligations and successor liability.

          - **Monitoring vendor transition** — continuity of transaction monitoring
          when Harbor''s SaaS contract terminates at close.

          - **Marketing compliance** — the $50 welcome bonus offer.


          The most decision-changing unknown is the **acquisition structure** (asset
          vs. stock vs. merger), because it determines whether Harbor''s licenses
          and regulatory obligations transfer to Mosaic or must be re-established.
          Please answer the four questions in the intake card — structure, KYC reliance,
          SAR/alerts status, and the new-market licensing plan — and I''ll build the
          issue map.'
        created_at: '2026-09-09T20:53:17+00:00'
        action_actor: null
        workspace_action: null
        conversation_id: CONV-20260909-5299cf
        path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/conversations/CONV-20260909-5299cf.md
