        available_excerpt: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe
          Harbor Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned
          Nov 15 close. This is the accepted working view. It is not a recorded decision.\n\nThis
          draft recommends separating the acquisition close from the launch of regulated
          services. The asset purchase can proceed while Mosaic prepares the migration.
          Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access on day one unless:\n\n1.
          Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in each affected
          state.\n2. Compliance approves reliance on Harbor’s know-your-customer (KYC)
          results or completes required remediation.\n3. Authorized reviewers assess
          Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report (SAR) history.\n4. Mosaic
          tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed and shows that it has
          no material coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic should hold
          the affected state launch, restrict affected accounts, or delay full product
          access. The planned $50 welcome bonus should wait until its structure, terms,
          funding, and disclosures are reviewed.\n\nNo decision has been recorded.\n\n###
          Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is subject to applicable state money-transmission
          and federal anti-money-laundering requirements. The licensing, KYC, alert,
          and monitoring answers depend on this unverified legal premise.\n- Mosaic
          will become the operating provider after close. This affects whether Harbor
          could remain the licensed provider during a transition.\n- The analysis
          does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer, that its KYC results satisfy
          Mosaic’s program, or that monitoring can continue without a gap.\n- The
          older assumption that the acquisition structure was unknown is superseded.
          The reported structure is an asset purchase.\n- Mosaic’s reported 41-state
          license footprint is a reported fact, not an assumption.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n-
          Harbor reportedly has licenses in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states,
          and the combined footprint is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states
          larger than Mosaic’s 41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition
          opens four new markets. This affects which states require separate authority
          or launch restrictions. The license lists and the intended meaning of “market”
          are needed.\n- Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The
          reported close is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake.
          A saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish
          the actual closing year. The operative close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n##
          Decision question\n\nDoes any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration
          need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n## Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045
          -->\n### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
          under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive
          the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should not treat Harbor’s
          money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically transfer in the
          reported asset purchase. Mosaic should not launch regulated services in
          a state without documented authority for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe
          acquisition may close separately from the service launch. A state launch
          hold is the current fallback where authority is not established.\n\n**Rule
          and support**\n\nSaved research concludes that the answer must be determined
          state by state. The review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction notices
          or approvals, interim operation, outstanding obligations, and Harbor’s license
          surrender.\n\nFour sources were retrieved, but no operative passage was
          selected, read, or verified. They do not establish the governing rule in
          any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
          [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n- [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n-
          [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n- [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n\nThe
          model act is not proof of any state’s adopted law. The premise that an asset
          purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority
          remains an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
          reportedly has licenses in 38 states. Mosaic reportedly has licenses in
          41 states. Their combined footprint is reported as 44 states. Mosaic plans
          to use or assume Harbor’s licenses in the new markets.\n\nThe unified Mosaic
          account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products suggest that Mosaic
          may become the actual provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity or licenses
          active might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could remain the
          licensed provider during a transition only if customer contracts, funds
          flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable state
          rules support that result. The written structure must match actual operations.\n\nA
          partner bank holding funds would not by itself resolve the issue. The result
          still depends on who contracts with users, controls transfers, owes repayment,
          records balances, resolves errors, and performs regulated duties.\n\n**Next
          step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only jurisdictions and complete a state matrix.
          For each state, determine Mosaic’s authority, required filings or approvals,
          operation while an application is pending, transfer of customer obligations,
          bank custody and control, Harbor’s run-off duties, and the required launch
          restriction if authority is not established.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start
          -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved
          research snapshot. Its facts and assumptions may predate later records.
          Use the current answer above for application to the current matter.\n\nDo
          not rely on transferability without an applicable state rule, approval,
          or written regulator position.\n\nThe answer must be determined state by
          state and must cover more than technical change-of-control rules.\n\nThis
          path is possible only if Harbor remains the real provider and the relevant
          states permit the arrangement. The unified Mosaic account design may conflict
          with that position.\n\nThe result depends on the contracts and actual funds
          flow. Custody alone should not be treated as a licensing exemption or transfer
          mechanism.\n\nResearch saved. 4 sources retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext
          step: Identify the four Harbor-only states and complete one matrix covering
          license authority, transaction filings, interim operation, bank custody,
          outstanding obligations, and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed
          analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
          transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
          Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated
          launch by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close.
          However, Mosaic should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only
          states unless one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own
          license.\n2. The state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3.
          The regulator confirms a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the
          real licensed provider under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks
          regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account
          is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service
          provider. If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses
          alive might not give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified operative
          authority retrieved.** The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission
          Modernization Act and a New York regulator licensing page. However, no exact
          provision about an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation, or custody
          was available for review. Also, a model act is not proof of the law adopted
          in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work
          needed before launch**\n\n| Work | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence
          to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Identify the four
          Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority gap | Licensing
          team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities | Block regulated
          functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every affected state |
          Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ | State regulatory
          counsel | Before the closing conditions are final | Applicable rule, filing
          deadline, regulator response, and license status | Delay migration in the
          affected state |\n| Confirm the post-close service provider | The licensed
          entity must match the actual operating model | Product and deal counsel
          | Before customer notices and account design are final | Contracts, user
          interface, funds-flow diagram, and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the
          actual provider where permitted |\n| Review notices and approvals | An asset
          sale can create separate seller and buyer requirements | Licensing team
          | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts and required approvals or
          non-objections | Make approval a state launch condition |\n| Confirm interim
          operating authority | A pending application should not be assumed to permit
          operation | State regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable rule or
          written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict
          transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody does not,
          by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel and
          bank relationship owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account
          titles, control rights, reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds
          and obligations in the existing structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and
          surrender plans | Harbor may retain duties for balances, claims, records,
          and reports | Harbor compliance and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational
          shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and continued bonds and financial coverage
          | Keep Harbor licensed and operational longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo
          not search only for a rule called “license transfer.” Review each state
          for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n- change of control;\n- change
          in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n- assignment of outstanding
          payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons, locations, or agents;\n-
          license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement assignment; and\n-
          movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset purchase might
          fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s ownership
          does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still need
          a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority before
          it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
          notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
          new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
          regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim
          operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition
          period. However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA
          supportable structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains
          responsible to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n-
          Harbor controls the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses,
          bonds, and financial coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding
          obligations remain covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints,
          and examinations.\n- Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational
          role is permitted.\n- The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant
          regulator permits or accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates
          tension with this approach. A single Mosaic account, one combined balance,
          and full access to Mosaic products make it harder to show that Harbor remains
          the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank custody**\n\nA partner bank account
          is not automatically a substitute for a money transmitter license. The key
          questions concern the complete activity and obligation flow.\n\nFor each
          customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives the customer’s
          instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit or return the funds?\n3.
          In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a custodial or “for benefit
          of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who owns the ledger and
          resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8. Which entity
          owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and permissible
          investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit assignment,
          migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required
          before closing or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic,
          or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different
          licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs
          only permitted services. A bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic
          or Harbor is different. The legal documents, customer terms, control rights,
          and actual operations must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n-
          account segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve
          funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n- continuity
          if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return and
          chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n-
          whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual account
          structure.\n\n**Recommended closing position**\n\nKeep the acquisition closing
          separate from the regulated-service launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only
          states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic has documented authority.
          For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing licenses cover the
          complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s
          licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit it
          and all outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed
          into an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change
          the current recommendation. It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody
          is part of the licensing analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority
          gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
          retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
          -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with missing
          underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's independent
          CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe present record does not
          support migration of all users without further review. Mosaic has KYC pass/fail
          results, but it lacks underlying documents for users onboarded before 2023.
          Compliance has not confirmed whether Mosaic’s anti-money-laundering and
          customer identification program (CIP) permits reliance on Harbor’s work.\n\nMosaic
          should restrict or re-verify affected users unless compliance documents
          a permitted reliance method and shows that the available records satisfy
          it.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched. The unverified
          legal premise is that an entity subject to federal anti-money-laundering
          and CIP duties must follow its own applicable program and recordkeeping
          requirements when it begins serving acquired customers.\n\nThe precise research
          question is whether Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s prior identification work
          after an asset purchase, what reliance conditions apply, and which records
          Mosaic must obtain or reproduce.\n\n**Application**\n\nMosaic plans to move
          240,000 consumer users and 12,000 business accounts into its app on day
          one without re-verification. The scale increases the effect of any program
          or record gap.\n\nA pass/fail result may show Harbor reached a conclusion.
          It does not establish what data Harbor collected, how Harbor verified identity,
          whether the information remains current, or whether Mosaic can produce required
          records.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program permits this form of reliance and the retained
          data meets the applicable requirements, targeted remediation may be enough.
          If it does not, affected users will require re-verification or restricted
          access before Mosaic provides services that require completed identification.\n\n**Next
          step**\n\nCompliance should issue a written decision that identifies the
          governing Mosaic program provisions, the available Harbor data, the missing
          evidence, and the remediation required for each user group. Product access
          rules must reflect that decision before migration.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
          -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
          retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38
          -->\n### SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
          Harbor's ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability\n\n**Current
          answer**\n\nAuthorized personnel should review the approximately 40 open
          alerts and the relevant SAR history before full migration. Their existence
          does not prove a violation or successor liability. Their unread status prevents
          Mosaic from assessing reportable activity, affected accounts, unresolved
          investigations, and deal or migration controls.\n\nThe asset-purchase structure
          does not by itself answer which entity must complete Harbor’s pending work
          or retain related records.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not
          been researched. The unverified legal questions are which entity must investigate
          pre-close activity, make any required SAR filing, retain records, and respond
          to later regulator requests after this asset purchase.\n\nSAR information
          can be subject to strict access and confidentiality limits. Diligence should
          therefore use personnel and procedures authorized to access it. A need for
          review is not an instruction to disclose or transfer restricted material
          outside a permitted process.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor has approximately
          40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last year. None has been
          reviewed in diligence.\n\nIf the alerts concern customers who will migrate,
          Mosaic may need account restrictions, enhanced review, or another control
          before giving them full access. If review finds unresolved reportable activity
          or serious program failures, the result could affect migration scope, contractual
          protections, or whether Harbor must complete work before close.\n\nIf the
          alerts are resolved as false positives and the SAR history shows no material
          control problem, a documented handoff may be sufficient. That result cannot
          be assumed from the current record.\n\n**Next step**\n\nUse an authorized
          review team to classify every open alert, identify any required pre-close
          action, and prepare a lawful handoff and retention plan. Escalate material
          findings into the deal and migration decision before affected accounts receive
          full access.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start
          -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
          retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542
          -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
          when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current answer**\n\nA day-one
          feed repoint is not enough by itself. Mosaic should validate that its engine
          receives complete, accurate, and timely Harbor transaction and customer
          data before migrated users receive unrestricted access.\n\nIf validation
          is incomplete, Mosaic should extend the existing service where possible,
          run both systems in parallel, or restrict activity until the replacement
          is shown to work.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched.
          The precise unverified legal question is what monitoring Mosaic and Harbor
          must maintain before, during, and after the transition under their applicable
          anti-money-laundering programs.\n\nIndependent of the final legal rule,
          end-to-end testing is a recommended risk control. It is not presented as
          a separately verified legal requirement.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
          monitoring contract ends at close. The plan is to repoint its transaction
          feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one. This creates a single transition point
          with no recorded overlap or completed validation.\n\nTesting must cover
          all relevant transaction types, customer identifiers, timestamps, amounts,
          status changes, rejected events, and alert generation. It must also address
          transactions that start before close and settle afterward.\n\nA successful
          connection test would not prove complete monitoring. Mosaic needs reconciliation
          and scenario testing that show the source data, rules, alerts, investigation
          workflow, and record retention work together.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete
          an end-to-end validation and reconciliation report before full access begins.
          The report should state tested coverage, known gaps, error handling, cutover
          ownership, and the fallback plan. A material unresolved gap should delay
          or restrict the affected activity.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start
          -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
          retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66
          -->\n### Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state
          money transmission or consumer protection implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe
          close-plus-one bonus campaign should wait for legal review. The record does
          not explain its eligibility rules, funding, payment method, exclusions,
          expiry, reversal rights, or disclosures.\n\nThe campaign should also wait
          until Mosaic knows which users and states can lawfully receive the underlying
          transfer service.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched.
          The unverified legal question is whether the final offer structure triggers
          state promotional, consumer-protection, money-transmission, unclaimed-property,
          tax, or related disclosure duties.\n\nA $50 payment is not automatically
          a deposit or interest payment. Its legal treatment depends on the actual
          offer and funds flow.\n\n**Application**\n\nMarketing wants to offer $50
          on a user’s first transfer at close plus one day. The meaning of “first
          transfer” and the conditions for earning or losing the bonus are unknown.\n\nThe
          offer could mislead users if it advertises service in a state where Mosaic
          cannot yet operate, omits material eligibility terms, or gives Mosaic broad
          discretion not clearly disclosed. It could also increase transaction volume
          during an unvalidated monitoring transition.\n\n**Next step**\n\nPrepare
          the complete offer terms and funds-flow description. Review the eligible
          users, states, qualifying transfer, payment timing, exclusions, reversals,
          expiry, complaint handling, and disclosures. Delay or narrow the campaign
          if licensing, KYC, or monitoring conditions remain unresolved.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start
          -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
          retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end -->\n\n## Alternatives
          considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4 -->\n### Bank-held
          funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
          this test only, a bank would hold the relevant funds. Mosaic would control
          transfer instructions, subject to completion of the bank contract and operating
          setup. Migration would occur on November 15, 2026, and bank integration
          would be ready on December 3, 2026. Pre-2023 identity documents would remain
          missing, 40 alert cases would remain pending, and monitoring would end at
          close.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nBank custody could provide a different operating
          structure for the licensing review. It could be useful if the bank becomes
          the actual provider and the contracts, customer terms, control rights, and
          operations support that role.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nOn the
          hypothetical dates, the bank integration is ready 18 days after migration.
          It therefore makes the November 15 migration harder unless readiness moves
          earlier or migration moves later.\n\nA new bank contract is not itself a
          disadvantage. The timing problem exists because the benefit depends on completing
          both the contract and operating setup before migration.\n\n**Issues that
          remain**\n\nBank custody does not resolve missing identity evidence, pending
          alerts, or the loss of monitoring at close. It also does not establish that
          Mosaic can use Harbor’s licenses or that Mosaic is outside state licensing
          rules while it controls transfer instructions.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe
          saved working note proposes that Mara Chen obtain a dated bank-readiness
          plan and determine whether the bank can support November 15. That scenario-only
          work should also assign resolution of the identity, alert, and monitoring
          gaps.\n\nUse this option only if the bank structure is legally supported
          and operationally ready before the selected migration date.\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6
          -->\n### Bank-held funds structure — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
          alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
          this test only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nThe
          structure could change the licensing analysis if the bank is the actual
          provider and Mosaic performs only activities that the law and bank agreement
          permit.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nCustody alone does not transfer
          Harbor’s licenses or establish Mosaic’s authority. A structure that names
          the bank as provider but leaves Mosaic in actual control could fail to achieve
          its intended benefit.\n\n**Issues that remain**\n\nThe alternative leaves
          open who contracts with users, controls transfer instructions and settlement,
          records balances, owes repayment, and handles KYC, monitoring, alerts, SARs,
          privacy, and marketing.\n\nIt does not resolve the current KYC evidence,
          alert-review, or monitoring gaps.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare customer-contract
          and funds-flow diagrams. Compare the legal documents with actual operational
          control. Use this option only if the bank’s role creates a supported legal
          path and does not delay the migration beyond the business objective.\n\n##
          Next actions\n\n1. **Review the open alerts and SAR history.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
          Authorized case review, account-impact list, filing assessment, and handoff
          plan.  \n   **Result needed:** Material cases are resolved or controlled
          before affected users receive full access.  \n   **Dependent activity:**
          Migration scope, account restrictions, and deal protections.  \n   **Fallback:**
          Restrict affected accounts, require Harbor to complete defined work, or
          delay their migration.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Harbor and Mosaic
          anti-money-laundering leads, with deal counsel, before the final migration
          decision.\n\n2. **Establish state operating authority.**  \n   **Deliverable:**
          Reconciled license lists and a state matrix for the complete post-close
          product and funds flow.  \n   **Result needed:** Documented authority, approval,
          or a lawful transition path in each launch state.  \n   **Dependent activity:**
          State launch, account migration, customer notices, and Harbor license surrender.
          \ \n   **Fallback:** Hold the affected state launch or keep Harbor as the
          actual provider where supported.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Licensing
          team and state regulatory counsel, before closing conditions and customer
          communications are final.\n\n3. **Resolve KYC reliance and missing records.**
          \ \n   **Deliverable:** Written compliance decision and user-segment remediation
          plan.  \n   **Result needed:** A supported basis to rely on Harbor’s KYC
          or completed re-verification for affected users.  \n   **Dependent activity:**
          Full account access and the no-reverification plan.  \n   **Fallback:**
          Restrict or re-verify affected users.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:**
          Mosaic compliance, before migration rules are locked.\n\n4. **Validate monitoring
          continuity.**  \n   **Deliverable:** End-to-end test, reconciliation report,
          and cutover fallback.  \n   **Result needed:** Complete and timely data
          ingestion, alert generation, investigation workflow, and record retention.
          \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Unrestricted post-close transactions.  \n
          \  **Fallback:** Extend Harbor’s service, run both systems, or restrict
          affected activity.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic compliance
          technology and operations, before cutover approval.\n\n5. **Review the $50
          bonus.**  \n   **Deliverable:** Final offer terms, funds flow, state scope,
          and disclosure review.  \n   **Result needed:** A clear and supportable
          promotion limited to users and states approved for launch.  \n   **Dependent
          activity:** Close-plus-one marketing campaign.  \n   **Fallback:** Delay
          or narrow the offer.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Marketing counsel
          and compliance, after launch scope is known and before publication.\n\n##
          Current work product and supporting records\n\n- [Known facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n-
          [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n- [Money transmission
          research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
          [Prior dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-3dc22f6f653187367a96.md)\n-
          [Bank-held funds timing test](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n-
          [Bank-held funds structure](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n[Open
          saved dossier revision](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/dossier-revisions/DOS-e1dcd612539ad45c6d6f.md)\n\nDossier
          generated and saved."

          role: assistant
          content: "# Harbor 2 matter dossier\n\n## Current position\n\nThe Harbor
            Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned Nov
            15 close. This is the accepted working view. It is not a recorded decision.\n\nThis
            draft recommends separating the acquisition close from the launch of regulated
            services. The asset purchase can proceed while Mosaic prepares the migration.
            Mosaic should not give all Harbor users full access on day one unless:\n\n1.
            Mosaic has documented authority for each post-close service in each affected
            state.\n2. Compliance approves reliance on Harbor’s know-your-customer
            (KYC) results or completes required remediation.\n3. Authorized reviewers
            assess Harbor’s open alerts and suspicious activity report (SAR) history.\n4.
            Mosaic tests the replacement transaction-monitoring feed and shows that
            it has no material coverage gap.\n\nIf a condition is not met, Mosaic
            should hold the affected state launch, restrict affected accounts, or
            delay full product access. The planned $50 welcome bonus should wait until
            its structure, terms, funding, and disclosures are reviewed.\n\nNo decision
            has been recorded.\n\n### Assumptions used\n\n- Harbor is subject to applicable
            state money-transmission and federal anti-money-laundering requirements.
            The licensing, KYC, alert, and monitoring answers depend on this unverified
            legal premise.\n- Mosaic will become the operating provider after close.
            This affects whether Harbor could remain the licensed provider during
            a transition.\n- The analysis does not assume that Harbor’s licenses transfer,
            that its KYC results satisfy Mosaic’s program, or that monitoring can
            continue without a gap.\n- The older assumption that the acquisition structure
            was unknown is superseded. The reported structure is an asset purchase.\n-
            Mosaic’s reported 41-state license footprint is a reported fact, not an
            assumption.\n\n### Record conflicts\n\n- Harbor reportedly has licenses
            in 38 states, Mosaic has licenses in 41 states, and the combined footprint
            is 44 states. A 44-state footprint is three states larger than Mosaic’s
            41-state footprint, but the record says the acquisition opens four new
            markets. This affects which states require separate authority or launch
            restrictions. The license lists and the intended meaning of “market” are
            needed.\n- Matter metadata gives a target date of `2026-09-11`. The reported
            close is “Nov 15,” approximately ten weeks after the Sept. 9 intake. A
            saved hypothetical uses November 15, 2026, but that does not establish
            the actual closing year. The operative close date and year remain unresolved.\n\n##
            Decision question\n\nDoes any part of the Harbor Pay acquisition migration
            need legal review before the Nov 15 close?\n\n## Issues\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045
            -->\n### Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
            under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor's MTLs transfer/survive
            the acquisition\n\n**Current answer**\n\nMosaic should not treat Harbor’s
            money transmitter licenses as assets that automatically transfer in the
            reported asset purchase. Mosaic should not launch regulated services in
            a state without documented authority for its complete post-close activity.\n\nThe
            acquisition may close separately from the service launch. A state launch
            hold is the current fallback where authority is not established.\n\n**Rule
            and support**\n\nSaved research concludes that the answer must be determined
            state by state. The review must cover Mosaic’s authority, transaction
            notices or approvals, interim operation, outstanding obligations, and
            Harbor’s license surrender.\n\nFour sources were retrieved, but no operative
            passage was selected, read, or verified. They do not establish the governing
            rule in any affected state:\n\n- [Money transmission research packet](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n-
            [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n- [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n-
            [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n- [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n\nThe
            model act is not proof of any state’s adopted law. The premise that an
            asset purchase does not automatically give Mosaic Harbor’s operating authority
            remains an unverified state-law conclusion.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
            reportedly has licenses in 38 states. Mosaic reportedly has licenses in
            41 states. Their combined footprint is reported as 44 states. Mosaic plans
            to use or assume Harbor’s licenses in the new markets.\n\nThe unified
            Mosaic account, combined balance, and access to Mosaic products suggest
            that Mosaic may become the actual provider. If so, keeping Harbor’s entity
            or licenses active might not authorize Mosaic’s conduct.\n\nHarbor could
            remain the licensed provider during a transition only if customer contracts,
            funds flow, operating control, licenses, bonds, records, and applicable
            state rules support that result. The written structure must match actual
            operations.\n\nA partner bank holding funds would not by itself resolve
            the issue. The result still depends on who contracts with users, controls
            transfers, owes repayment, records balances, resolves errors, and performs
            regulated duties.\n\n**Next step**\n\nIdentify the Harbor-only jurisdictions
            and complete a state matrix. For each state, determine Mosaic’s authority,
            required filings or approvals, operation while an application is pending,
            transfer of customer obligations, bank custody and control, Harbor’s run-off
            duties, and the required launch restriction if authority is not established.\n\n<!--
            retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:start -->\n<details>\n<summary>Saved
            research and prior analysis</summary>\n\nPreserved research snapshot.
            Its facts and assumptions may predate later records. Use the current answer
            above for application to the current matter.\n\nDo not rely on transferability
            without an applicable state rule, approval, or written regulator position.\n\nThe
            answer must be determined state by state and must cover more than technical
            change-of-control rules.\n\nThis path is possible only if Harbor remains
            the real provider and the relevant states permit the arrangement. The
            unified Mosaic account design may conflict with that position.\n\nThe
            result depends on the contracts and actual funds flow. Custody alone should
            not be treated as a licensing exemption or transfer mechanism.\n\nResearch
            saved. 4 sources retrieved; 0 with passages read.\n\nNext step: Identify
            the four Harbor-only states and complete one matrix covering license authority,
            transaction filings, interim operation, bank custody, outstanding obligations,
            and license surrender.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Detailed analysis</summary>\n\n**Practical
            answer**\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money transmitter licenses as assets
            that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.** Use this closing rule:\n\n>
            **No confirmed authority means no regulated launch by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe
            asset purchase can still close. However, Mosaic should not activate regulated
            services in the four Harbor-only states unless one of these conditions
            is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own license.\n2. The state approves a
            transfer or other license change.\n3. The regulator confirms a lawful
            interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the real licensed provider under
            a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks regulated functions in that
            state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account is important. It suggests
            that Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service provider. If that is
            correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses alive might not give
            Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified operative authority retrieved.**
            The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act
            and a New York regulator licensing page. However, no exact provision about
            an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation, or custody was available
            for review. Also, a model act is not proof of the law adopted in a specific
            state. The state-specific conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n**Work
            needed before launch**\n\n| Work | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by |
            Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Identify
            the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority
            gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities
            | Block regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every
            affected state | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ
            | State regulatory counsel | Before the closing conditions are final |
            Applicable rule, filing deadline, regulator response, and license status
            | Delay migration in the affected state |\n| Confirm the post-close service
            provider | The licensed entity must match the actual operating model |
            Product and deal counsel | Before customer notices and account design
            are final | Contracts, user interface, funds-flow diagram, and operating
            roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider where permitted |\n| Review
            notices and approvals | An asset sale can create separate seller and buyer
            requirements | Licensing team | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts
            and required approvals or non-objections | Make approval a state launch
            condition |\n| Confirm interim operating authority | A pending application
            should not be assumed to permit operation | State regulatory counsel |
            Before close | Applicable rule or written regulator confirmation | Keep
            Harbor customers segregated or restrict transactions |\n| Review partner-bank
            arrangements | Bank custody does not, by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing
            position | Payments counsel and bank relationship owner | Before balances
            move | Bank agreements, account titles, control rights, reconciliation
            design, and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations in the existing
            structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and surrender plans | Harbor may
            retain duties for balances, claims, records, and reports | Harbor compliance
            and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational shutdown | Regulator-approved
            plan and continued bonds and financial coverage | Keep Harbor licensed
            and operational longer |\n\n**State notice and approval**\n\nDo not search
            only for a rule called “license transfer.” Review each state for:\n\n-
            sale of substantially all assets;\n- change of control;\n- change in business
            plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n- assignment of outstanding payment
            obligations;\n- change in responsible persons, locations, or agents;\n-
            license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement assignment; and\n-
            movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset purchase might
            fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s ownership
            does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still need
            a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority
            before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
            notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
            new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
            regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n**Interim
            operation**\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition
            period. However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA
            supportable structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains
            responsible to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n-
            Harbor controls the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses,
            bonds, and financial coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding
            obligations remain covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints,
            and examinations.\n- Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational
            role is permitted.\n- The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each
            relevant regulator permits or accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan
            creates tension with this approach. A single Mosaic account, one combined
            balance, and full access to Mosaic products make it harder to show that
            Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n**Partner-bank custody**\n\nA partner
            bank account is not automatically a substitute for a money transmitter
            license. The key questions concern the complete activity and obligation
            flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives
            the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit
            or return the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is
            it a custodial or “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6.
            Who owns the ledger and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer
            fails?\n8. Which entity owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s
            license, bond, and permissible investments cover the obligation?\n10.
            Does the bank agreement permit assignment, migration, or a change in the
            program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required before closing or migration?\n12.
            What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA
            bank-led model might provide a different licensing analysis if the bank
            is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. A
            bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different.
            The legal documents, customer terms, control rights, and actual operations
            must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account segregation;\n-
            daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve funding;\n- bank setoff
            rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n- continuity if the account
            is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return and chargeback
            duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n- whether
            any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual account structure.\n\n**Recommended
            closing position**\n\nKeep the acquisition closing separate from the regulated-service
            launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only states, use a state launch hold unless
            Mosaic has documented authority. For overlapping states, confirm that
            Mosaic’s existing licenses cover the complete post-close product set and
            funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s licenses or release its bonds
            until the applicable regulators permit it and all outstanding obligations
            have been assigned, completed, or placed into an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis
            investigation does not change the current recommendation. It adds one
            material point: **partner-bank custody is part of the licensing analysis,
            but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n</details>\n\nResearch
            history: [Saved research 1](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md)\n\n</details>\n<!--
            retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-94e42e2b38090045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045
            -->\n### BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor's prior KYC (with
            missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic Relay's
            independent CIP/AML obligations\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe present record
            does not support migration of all users without further review. Mosaic
            has KYC pass/fail results, but it lacks underlying documents for users
            onboarded before 2023. Compliance has not confirmed whether Mosaic’s anti-money-laundering
            and customer identification program (CIP) permits reliance on Harbor’s
            work.\n\nMosaic should restrict or re-verify affected users unless compliance
            documents a permitted reliance method and shows that the available records
            satisfy it.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched.
            The unverified legal premise is that an entity subject to federal anti-money-laundering
            and CIP duties must follow its own applicable program and recordkeeping
            requirements when it begins serving acquired customers.\n\nThe precise
            research question is whether Mosaic may rely on Harbor’s prior identification
            work after an asset purchase, what reliance conditions apply, and which
            records Mosaic must obtain or reproduce.\n\n**Application**\n\nMosaic
            plans to move 240,000 consumer users and 12,000 business accounts into
            its app on day one without re-verification. The scale increases the effect
            of any program or record gap.\n\nA pass/fail result may show Harbor reached
            a conclusion. It does not establish what data Harbor collected, how Harbor
            verified identity, whether the information remains current, or whether
            Mosaic can produce required records.\n\nIf Mosaic’s program permits this
            form of reliance and the retained data meets the applicable requirements,
            targeted remediation may be enough. If it does not, affected users will
            require re-verification or restricted access before Mosaic provides services
            that require completed identification.\n\n**Next step**\n\nCompliance
            should issue a written decision that identifies the governing Mosaic program
            provisions, the available Harbor data, the missing evidence, and the remediation
            required for each user group. Product access rules must reflect that decision
            before migration.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:start
            -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
            retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-ca95e529feeb1045:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38
            -->\n### SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
            Harbor's ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability\n\n**Current
            answer**\n\nAuthorized personnel should review the approximately 40 open
            alerts and the relevant SAR history before full migration. Their existence
            does not prove a violation or successor liability. Their unread status
            prevents Mosaic from assessing reportable activity, affected accounts,
            unresolved investigations, and deal or migration controls.\n\nThe asset-purchase
            structure does not by itself answer which entity must complete Harbor’s
            pending work or retain related records.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis
            issue has not been researched. The unverified legal questions are which
            entity must investigate pre-close activity, make any required SAR filing,
            retain records, and respond to later regulator requests after this asset
            purchase.\n\nSAR information can be subject to strict access and confidentiality
            limits. Diligence should therefore use personnel and procedures authorized
            to access it. A need for review is not an instruction to disclose or transfer
            restricted material outside a permitted process.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor
            has approximately 40 open alerts and “a handful” of SARs from the last
            year. None has been reviewed in diligence.\n\nIf the alerts concern customers
            who will migrate, Mosaic may need account restrictions, enhanced review,
            or another control before giving them full access. If review finds unresolved
            reportable activity or serious program failures, the result could affect
            migration scope, contractual protections, or whether Harbor must complete
            work before close.\n\nIf the alerts are resolved as false positives and
            the SAR history shows no material control problem, a documented handoff
            may be sufficient. That result cannot be assumed from the current record.\n\n**Next
            step**\n\nUse an authorized review team to classify every open alert,
            identify any required pre-close action, and prepare a lawful handoff and
            retention plan. Escalate material findings into the deal and migration
            decision before affected accounts receive full access.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:start
            -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
            retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-69af3f282d21ef38:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542
            -->\n### Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
            when the SaaS contract terminates at close\n\n**Current answer**\n\nA
            day-one feed repoint is not enough by itself. Mosaic should validate that
            its engine receives complete, accurate, and timely Harbor transaction
            and customer data before migrated users receive unrestricted access.\n\nIf
            validation is incomplete, Mosaic should extend the existing service where
            possible, run both systems in parallel, or restrict activity until the
            replacement is shown to work.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has
            not been researched. The precise unverified legal question is what monitoring
            Mosaic and Harbor must maintain before, during, and after the transition
            under their applicable anti-money-laundering programs.\n\nIndependent
            of the final legal rule, end-to-end testing is a recommended risk control.
            It is not presented as a separately verified legal requirement.\n\n**Application**\n\nHarbor’s
            monitoring contract ends at close. The plan is to repoint its transaction
            feed to Mosaic’s engine on day one. This creates a single transition point
            with no recorded overlap or completed validation.\n\nTesting must cover
            all relevant transaction types, customer identifiers, timestamps, amounts,
            status changes, rejected events, and alert generation. It must also address
            transactions that start before close and settle afterward.\n\nA successful
            connection test would not prove complete monitoring. Mosaic needs reconciliation
            and scenario testing that show the source data, rules, alerts, investigation
            workflow, and record retention work together.\n\n**Next step**\n\nComplete
            an end-to-end validation and reconciliation report before full access
            begins. The report should state tested coverage, known gaps, error handling,
            cutover ownership, and the fallback plan. A material unresolved gap should
            delay or restrict the affected activity.\n\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:start
            -->\nInitial analysis — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!--
            retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-4825f0af7ec75542:end -->\n\n<!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66
            -->\n### Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any state
            money transmission or consumer protection implications\n\n**Current answer**\n\nThe
            close-plus-one bonus campaign should wait for legal review. The record
            does not explain its eligibility rules, funding, payment method, exclusions,
            expiry, reversal rights, or disclosures.\n\nThe campaign should also wait
            until Mosaic knows which users and states can lawfully receive the underlying
            transfer service.\n\n**Rule and support**\n\nThis issue has not been researched.
            The unverified legal question is whether the final offer structure triggers
            state promotional, consumer-protection, money-transmission, unclaimed-property,
            tax, or related disclosure duties.\n\nA $50 payment is not automatically
            a deposit or interest payment. Its legal treatment depends on the actual
            offer and funds flow.\n\n**Application**\n\nMarketing wants to offer $50
            on a user’s first transfer at close plus one day. The meaning of “first
            transfer” and the conditions for earning or losing the bonus are unknown.\n\nThe
            offer could mislead users if it advertises service in a state where Mosaic
            cannot yet operate, omits material eligibility terms, or gives Mosaic
            broad discretion not clearly disclosed. It could also increase transaction
            volume during an unvalidated monitoring transition.\n\n**Next step**\n\nPrepare
            the complete offer terms and funds-flow description. Review the eligible
            users, states, qualifying transfer, payment timing, exclusions, reversals,
            expiry, complaint handling, and disclosures. Delay or narrow the campaign
            if licensing, KYC, or monitoring conditions remain unresolved.\n\n<!--
            retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:start -->\nInitial analysis
            — no completed research is saved for this issue.\n<!-- retained-issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-72810d0a43d3ce66:end
            -->\n\n## Alternatives considered\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4
            -->\n### Bank-held funds timing test — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
            alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-0f23edfc89ec6ecaf60a13e4.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
            this test only, a bank would hold the relevant funds. Mosaic would control
            transfer instructions, subject to completion of the bank contract and
            operating setup. Migration would occur on November 15, 2026, and bank
            integration would be ready on December 3, 2026. Pre-2023 identity documents
            would remain missing, 40 alert cases would remain pending, and monitoring
            would end at close.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nBank custody could provide a different
            operating structure for the licensing review. It could be useful if the
            bank becomes the actual provider and the contracts, customer terms, control
            rights, and operations support that role.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nOn
            the hypothetical dates, the bank integration is ready 18 days after migration.
            It therefore makes the November 15 migration harder unless readiness moves
            earlier or migration moves later.\n\nA new bank contract is not itself
            a disadvantage. The timing problem exists because the benefit depends
            on completing both the contract and operating setup before migration.\n\n**Issues
            that remain**\n\nBank custody does not resolve missing identity evidence,
            pending alerts, or the loss of monitoring at close. It also does not establish
            that Mosaic can use Harbor’s licenses or that Mosaic is outside state
            licensing rules while it controls transfer instructions.\n\n**Next action**\n\nThe
            saved working note proposes that Mara Chen obtain a dated bank-readiness
            plan and determine whether the bank can support November 15. That scenario-only
            work should also assign resolution of the identity, alert, and monitoring
            gaps.\n\nUse this option only if the bank structure is legally supported
            and operationally ready before the selected migration date.\n\n<!-- alternative:SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6
            -->\n### Bank-held funds structure — **Hypothetical — not adopted**\n\n[Saved
            alternative](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/scenarios/SCN-406906c91ab0aba4313b54a6.md)\n\n**Assumptions**\n\nFor
            this test only, a partner bank holds customer funds.\n\n**Benefits**\n\nThe
            structure could change the licensing analysis if the bank is the actual
            provider and Mosaic performs only activities that the law and bank agreement
            permit.\n\n**Trade-offs and added risks**\n\nCustody alone does not transfer
            Harbor’s licenses or establish Mosaic’s authority. A structure that names
            the bank as provider but leaves Mosaic in actual control could fail to
            achieve its intended benefit.\n\n**Issues that remain**\n\nThe alternative
            leaves open who contracts with users, controls transfer instructions and
            settlement, records balances, owes repayment, and handles KYC, monitoring,
            alerts, SARs, privacy, and marketing.\n\nIt does not resolve the current
            KYC evidence, alert-review, or monitoring gaps.\n\n**Next action**\n\nPrepare
            customer-contract and funds-flow diagrams. Compare the legal documents
            with actual operational control. Use this option only if the bank’s role
            creates a supported legal path and does not delay the migration beyond
            the business objective.\n\n## Next actions\n\n1. **Review the open alerts
            and SAR history.**  \n   **Deliverable:** Authorized case review, account-impact
            list, filing assessment, and handoff plan.  \n   **Result needed:** Material
            cases are resolved or controlled before affected users receive full access.
            \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Migration scope, account restrictions,
            and deal protections.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict affected accounts,
            require Harbor to complete defined work, or delay their migration.  \n
            \  **Proposed owner and timing:** Harbor and Mosaic anti-money-laundering
            leads, with deal counsel, before the final migration decision.\n\n2. **Establish
            state operating authority.**  \n   **Deliverable:** Reconciled license
            lists and a state matrix for the complete post-close product and funds
            flow.  \n   **Result needed:** Documented authority, approval, or a lawful
            transition path in each launch state.  \n   **Dependent activity:** State
            launch, account migration, customer notices, and Harbor license surrender.
            \ \n   **Fallback:** Hold the affected state launch or keep Harbor as
            the actual provider where supported.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:**
            Licensing team and state regulatory counsel, before closing conditions
            and customer communications are final.\n\n3. **Resolve KYC reliance and
            missing records.**  \n   **Deliverable:** Written compliance decision
            and user-segment remediation plan.  \n   **Result needed:** A supported
            basis to rely on Harbor’s KYC or completed re-verification for affected
            users.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Full account access and the no-reverification
            plan.  \n   **Fallback:** Restrict or re-verify affected users.  \n   **Proposed
            owner and timing:** Mosaic compliance, before migration rules are locked.\n\n4.
            **Validate monitoring continuity.**  \n   **Deliverable:** End-to-end
            test, reconciliation report, and cutover fallback.  \n   **Result needed:**
            Complete and timely data ingestion, alert generation, investigation workflow,
            and record retention.  \n   **Dependent activity:** Unrestricted post-close
            transactions.  \n   **Fallback:** Extend Harbor’s service, run both systems,
            or restrict affected activity.  \n   **Proposed owner and timing:** Mosaic
            compliance technology and operations, before cutover approval.\n\n5. **Review
            the $50 bonus.**  \n   **Deliverable:** Final offer terms, funds flow,
            state scope, and disclosure review.  \n   **Result needed:** A clear and
            supportable promotion limited to users and states approved for launch.
            \ \n   **Dependent activity:** Close-plus-one marketing campaign.  \n
            \  **Fallback:** Delay or narrow the offer.  \n   **Proposed owner and
            timing:** Marketing counsel and compliance, after launch scope is known
            and before publication.\n\n## Current work product and supporting records\n\n-
            [Known facts](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md)\n- [Original request](03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/request.md)\n-
