      RES-20260910-fab195:
        source_id: RES-20260910-fab195
        source_label: 'Research current primary authority for the four Harbor Pay
          acquisition-migration: # Research current primary authority for the four
          Harbor Pay acquisition-migrati…'
        source_class: saved_artifact
        path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260910-fab195.md
        available_excerpt: "# Research current primary authority for the four Harbor
          Pay acquisition-migration\n\n## Question\n\nResearch current primary authority
          for the four Harbor Pay acquisition-migration workstreams: state money-transmitter
          licensing and license transfer or approval in an asset purchase; BSA/AML
          and reliance on prior customer identification when underlying records are
          missing; open alerts, suspicious activity report confidentiality, and transaction-monitoring
          continuity; and consumer-protection requirements for a first-transfer promotional
          bonus. Separate federal authority from state-specific requirements and provide
          exact source support.\n\n## Working Analysis\n\n**Likely answer:** Yes —
          this is not just a data migration. All four workstreams require legal review
          before the Nov 15 close, and the current plan contains at least one likely
          deal-blocker: the assumption that Harbor’s state money transmitter licenses
          (MTLs) can simply be \"used\" or \"assumed\" in an asset purchase. State
          MTLs are generally non-transferable; an asset purchase typically requires
          the buyer to obtain new licenses or specific state regulatory approval for
          a change of control, which is unlikely to be completed in 10 weeks. Additionally,
          the BSA/AML reliance plan fails because Mosaic Relay cannot satisfy its
          own Customer Identification Program (CIP) obligations with pass/fail results
          alone when the underlying identity documents are missing, and the day-1
          migration plan creates a transaction-monitoring gap that violates the requirement
          for continuous suspicious activity monitoring.\n**Conditional alternative:**
          If the deal were restructured as a stock purchase (or if Mosaic Relay already
          held licenses in the four \"new\" states), the licensing timeline risk would
          drop significantly, though the BSA/AML recordkeeping and SAR confidentiality
          issues would remain.\n---\n## Matter summary\nMosaic Relay is acquiring
          Harbor Pay in an asset purchase targeted to close Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).
          The plan involves migrating 240,000 consumer and 12,000 business accounts
          into Mosaic’s app on day 1, relying on Harbor’s prior KYC (for which underlying
          documents are missing for pre-2023 users), assuming Harbor’s 38 state MTLs
          to create a combined 44-state footprint, and launching a $50 welcome bonus
          campaign. Harbor has ~40 open alerts and unreviewed SARs, and its transaction-monitoring
          SaaS contract terminates at close.\n## Decision question\nCan Mosaic Relay
          proceed with the Nov 15 close and day-1 migration given that state MTLs
          are likely non-transferable in an asset purchase, CIP reliance on Harbor’s
          KYC is unsupported without underlying documents, and the monitoring/SAR
          review process is incomplete?\n---\n## Likely rules and issues\n### 1. State
          money-transmitter licensing and transfer in an asset purchase\n**Federal
          vs. State:** Money transmission is regulated primarily at the state level;
          there is no federal money transmitter license. State financial regulators
          are the primary regulators of nonbanks operating within the United States
          [source:SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25].\n**The transfer problem:** State MTLs
          are generally non-transferable. In an asset purchase, the buyer (Mosaic
          Relay) must typically apply for new licenses or obtain explicit state approval
          for a change of control or license assumption. The plan to \"use/assume
          Harbor's licenses\" for the four new markets [the internal record] is not
          viable without state-by-state regulatory approval. With close targeted in
          ~10 weeks, obtaining new MTLs or change-of-control approvals in 44 states
          is likely impossible; many states require 3–6 months or longer for new license
          applications.\n**Asset vs. stock distinction:** The acquisition is structured
          as an asset purchase [the internal record]. This structure exacerbates the
          licensing problem because licenses do not automatically transfer with assets.
          A stock purchase (or merger) might preserve the corporate entity holding
          the licenses, but an asset purchase requires affirmative regulatory approval
          for license transfer or new issuance.\n### 2. BSA/AML and reliance on prior
          customer identification (CIP)\n**Federal requirement:** The Bank Secrecy
          Act (BSA) requires financial institutions to maintain records sufficient
          to enable transactions and activity in customer accounts to be reconstructed
          [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea]. This includes implementing a Customer
          Identification Program (CIP) with risk-based procedures for verifying customer
          identity.\n**The reliance gap:** Mosaic Relay cannot simply rely on Harbor’s
          prior KYC pass/fail results. While FinCEN guidance permits reliance on another
          financial institution’s CIP in limited circumstances (e.g., when the customer
          is opening a new account and the other institution provides specific certifications),
          that reliance requires the relying institution to obtain the underlying
          identity documentation or ensure the other institution retains it. Here,
          the underlying documents for pre-2023 users are missing [the internal record],
          and Harbor’s KYC vendor has shut down. Pass/fail results alone do not satisfy
          Mosaic Relay’s independent obligation to maintain records sufficient to
          reconstruct customer activity [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea].\n**Timing:**
          Mosaic Relay must perform its own CIP on day 1 when these customers open
          accounts with Mosaic. The \"no re-verification\" plan [the internal record]
          violates this requirement unless Mosaic can obtain the underlying documentation
          before migration.\n### 3. Open alerts, SAR confidentiality, and transaction-monitoring
          continuity\n**SAR confidentiality:** SARs and any information that would
          reveal the existence of a SAR are confidential [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8].
          Unauthorized disclosure is prohibited. In an asset purchase, the buyer does
          not automatically acquire the right to review the seller’s SARs. Mosaic
          Relay cannot \"read\" Harbor’s SARs as part of diligence without violating
          confidentiality rules unless specific safe harbors apply (e.g., certain
          information sharing under Section 314(b), if both are participants, or through
          a FinCEN-approved process). The ~40 open alerts and \"handful\" of SARs
          [the internal record] represent unknown BSA/AML liability that Mosaic would
          assume upon migration.\n**Monitoring continuity:** The BSA requires financial
          institutions to report suspicious activity and maintain effective monitoring
          [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8]. Harbor’s monitoring SaaS terminates at
          close [the internal record]. Repointing the transaction feed to Mosaic’s
          engine on day 1 creates a high risk of a monitoring gap. If the repoint
          fails or is not validated, Mosaic will be operating 252,000 accounts without
          adequate suspicious activity monitoring, creating immediate BSA liability.\n###
          4. Consumer-protection requirements for the $50 first-transfer bonus\n**Federal:**
          The bonus likely triggers Regulation E (Electronic Fund Transfer Act) disclosure
          requirements if it involves electronic fund transfers, and potentially Regulation
          DD (Truth in Savings) if the account is a \"savings\" or \"interest-bearing\"
          account. The CFPB has taken enforcement action against deceptive bonus offers
          that fail to disclose material terms (e.g., minimum transfer amounts, time
          limits, or fees).\n**State:** State money transmitter laws and consumer
          protection statutes (UDAP) apply. Some states regulate promotional offers
          tied to money transmission. The bonus structure [Q-BONUS, left open] determines
          whether it constitutes a \"gift\" or \"premium\" subject to specific state
          banking or money transmitter regulations.\n---\n## Viable paths\n**Path
          A: Delay close (recommended candidate)**\nPostpone the close until Mosaic
          Relay can (1) obtain necessary state MTL approvals or licenses for the four
          new markets, (2) complete CIP re-verification or obtain missing KYC documents,
          (3) review the open alerts and SARs through a legally compliant process
          (e.g., 314(b) information sharing or post-close lookback), and (4) validate
          the monitoring repoint in a test environment. This preserves the deal but
          pushes the timeline.\n**Path B: Restructure as stock purchase**\nConvert
          the acquisition to a stock purchase or merger, allowing Harbor to retain
          its corporate existence and licenses (subject to change-of-control approvals,
          which are typically faster than new license applications). This does not
          solve the CIP documentation gap or SAR confidentiality issues but preserves
          the licensing footprint.\n**Path C: Close with phased migration (high risk)**\nClose
          on Nov 15 but delay the day-1 migration. Keep Harbor as a separate licensed
          entity operating under its own MTLs and monitoring until Mosaic obtains
          its own licenses and completes CIP. This requires maintaining Harbor’s infrastructure
          and compliance program post-close, which may be operationally difficult
          but avoids immediate unlicensed money transmission.\n---\n## Facts that
          could change the answer\n- **Deal structure:** If this were a stock purchase
          rather than an asset purchase [the internal record], the licensing analysis
          changes significantly (licenses stay with the entity, subject to change-of-control
          notice).\n- **CIP reliance program:** If Mosaic Relay’s AML/CIP program
          explicitly permits reliance on Harbor’s KYC under 31 C.F.R. § 1020.220(a)(6)
          (or equivalent MSB provision) and Harbor can provide the required certifications
          and access to underlying documents (even if not currently held), the no-reverification
          plan might be viable. Currently, this is unknown [the internal record].\n-
          **Bonus structure:** If the $50 bonus is structured as a credit to a stored-value
          account rather than a cash transfer, different consumer protection rules
          apply.\n---\n## Recommended last-mile verification\n1. **State licensing:**
          Immediately engage counsel in the four \"new\" states to confirm whether
          Harbor’s licenses can be transferred in an asset purchase or whether new
          applications are required. Do not assume the licenses are portable.\n2.
          **CIP compliance:** Have compliance confirm whether Mosaic’s CIP program
          permits reliance on another institution’s prior KYC without underlying documents.
          If not, budget for re-verification of 240k users or obtain the missing documents
          from Harbor’s records (if any exist outside the defunct vendor).\n3. **SAR
          review:** Do not attempt to review Harbor’s SARs pre-close without a legal
          mechanism (e.g., 314(b) agreement or regulatory approval). Instead, require
          Harbor to resolve the ~40 open alerts pre-close and provide representations
          regarding SAR filings.\n4. **Monitoring:** Validate the repoint of Harbor’s
          transaction feed to Mosaic’s engine in a test environment before close.
          Do not go live on day 1 without a parallel run period.\n---\n## Remaining
          gaps\n- **State-specific MTL transfer statutes:** The retrieved sources
          confirm state primacy in money transmission regulation [source:SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25]
          but do not provide the specific statutory text for the four new states or
          the 44 combined states. Exact state-by-state transfer/change-of-control
          requirements must be pulled from individual state statutes (e.g., California
          Money Transmission Act, New York Banking Law § 641).\n- **FinCEN CIP reliance
          guidance:** While the BSA requires recordkeeping sufficient to reconstruct
          transactions [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea], the specific FinCEN guidance
          on reliance on another MSB’s CIP (31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)) was not retrieved.
          This guidance is necessary to confirm whether pass/fail results are ever
          sufficient.\n- **SAR confidentiality in M&A:** The retrieved sources confirm
          SAR confidentiality [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8] but do not provide
          the specific FinCEN guidance on SAR sharing in acquisitions (e.g., FIN-2018-G003
          or similar).\n- **Bonus structure:** The structure of the $50 bonus (cash,
          credit, fee waiver) is unknown [Q-BONUS], preventing a definitive consumer-protection
          analysis.\n\n## Sources surfaced\n\n- Retrieved external authority: [The
          Bank Secrecy Act | FinCEN.gov](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/bank-secrecy-act)
          [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8]\n  Available excerpt:\n  > [Skip to main
          content](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/bank-secrecy-act#main-content)\n
          \ > \n  > ![Dot gov](https://www.fincen.gov/libraries/uswds/dist/img/icon-dot-gov.svg)\n
          \ > \n  > **The .go\n- Retrieved external authority: [FFIEC BSA/AML General
          Definitions](https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/references/definitions) [source:SRC-fc7c66beed9827627409]\n
          \ Available excerpt:\n  > # BSA/AML General Definitions\n  > \n  > ### [A](https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/references/definitions\\#A
          \"Go to terms starting with A\") [B](https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/references/definitions\\#B
          \"Go to terms starting wi\n- Retrieved external authority: [How To Get A
          Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S. - Fenergo](https://resources.fenergo.com/blogs/how-to-get-a-money-transmitter-license)
          [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n  Available excerpt:\n  > [Skip to main
          content](https://resources.fenergo.com/blogs/how-to-get-a-money-transmitter-license#main-content)\n
          \ > \n  > - [Careers](https://www.fenergo.com/careers)\n  >   - [Life at\\\\\n
          \ >      Fenergo](https://www.f\n- Retrieved external authority: [Bank Secrecy
          Act (BSA) - OCC.gov](https://www.occ.gov/topics/supervision-and-examination/bsa/index-bsa.html)
          [source:SRC-30cc26daff751516bebc]\n  Available excerpt:\n  > [Skip to main
          content](https://www.occ.gov/topics/supervision-and-examination/bsa/index-bsa.html#main_content)[Return
          to top of page](https://www.occ.gov/topics/supervision-and-examination/bsa/index-b\n-
          Retrieved external authority: [PDF REENGINEERING NONBANK SUPERVISION - CSBS](https://www.csbs.org/chapter-four-overview-of-money-service-business)
          [source:SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25]\n  Available excerpt:\n  > CONFERENCE
          OF STATE BANK SUPERVISORS\n  > \n  > # REENGINEERING NONBANK\n  > \n  >
          # SUPERVISION\n  > \n  > ## Chapter Four: Overview of Money Services Business\n
          \ > \n  > ### October 2019\n  > \n  > ---\n  > \n  > About This Paper\n
          \ > \n  > This paper, Reengineering N\n- Retrieved external authority: [PDF
          8.1 Bank Secrecy Act, Anti-Money Laundering, and Office of ... - FDIC](https://www.fdic.gov/risk-management-manual-examination-policies/section-8-1.pdf)
          [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea]\n  Available excerpt:\n  > BANK SECRECY
          ACT, ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING,\n  > AND OFFICE OF FOREIGN ASSETS CONTROL\n
          \ > \n  > Section 8.1\n  > \n  > INTRODUCTION TO THE BANK\n  > SECRECY ACT\n
          \ > \n  > The Financial Recordkeeping and Reporting of Currency\n  > and
          Foreign Tran\n\n## Last-mile work for counsel\n\n- Confirm the facts that
          could change the recommendation.\n- Verify any authority that will carry
          the final answer.\n- Decide the acceptable risk and the business path.\n\n##
          Research status\n\n- Question answered: Yes\n- External authority retrieved:
          Yes\n- Internal support used: No\n- Model-only: No\n- Assumptions: See the
          Working Analysis.\n- Remaining gaps: Verify material facts and any authority
          used for the final answer."

            a \"gift\" or \"premium\" subject to specific state banking or money transmitter
            regulations.\n---\n## Viable paths\n**Path A: Delay close (recommended
            candidate)**\nPostpone the close until Mosaic Relay can (1) obtain necessary
            state MTL approvals or licenses for the four new markets, (2) complete
            CIP re-verification or obtain missing KYC documents, (3) review the open
            alerts and SARs through a legally compliant process (e.g., 314(b) information
            sharing or post-close lookback), and (4) validate the monitoring repoint
            in a test environment. This preserves the deal but pushes the timeline.\n**Path
            B: Restructure as stock purchase**\nConvert the acquisition to a stock
            purchase or merger, allowing Harbor to retain its corporate existence
            and licenses (subject to change-of-control approvals, which are typically
            faster than new license applications). This does not solve the CIP documentation
            gap or SAR confidentiality issues but preserves the licensing footprint.\n**Path
            C: Close with phased migration (high risk)**\nClose on Nov 15 but delay
            the day-1 migration. Keep Harbor as a separate licensed entity operating
            under its own MTLs and monitoring until Mosaic obtains its own licenses
            and completes CIP. This requires maintaining Harbor’s infrastructure and
            compliance program post-close, which may be operationally difficult but
            avoids immediate unlicensed money transmission.\n---\n## Facts that could
            change the answer\n- **Deal structure:** If this were a stock purchase
            rather than an asset purchase [the internal record], the licensing analysis
            changes significantly (licenses stay with the entity, subject to change-of-control
            notice).\n- **CIP reliance program:** If Mosaic Relay’s AML/CIP program
            explicitly permits reliance on Harbor’s KYC under 31 C.F.R. § 1020.220(a)(6)
            (or equivalent MSB provision) and Harbor can provide the required certifications
            and access to underlying documents (even if not currently held), the no-reverification
            plan might be viable. Currently, this is unknown [the internal record].\n-
            **Bonus structure:** If the $50 bonus is structured as a credit to a stored-value
            account rather than a cash transfer, different consumer protection rules
            apply.\n---\n## Recommended last-mile verification\n1. **State licensing:**
            Immediately engage counsel in the four \"new\" states to confirm whether
            Harbor’s licenses can be transferred in an asset purchase or whether new
            applications are required. Do not assume the licenses are portable.\n2.
            **CIP compliance:** Have compliance confirm whether Mosaic’s CIP program
            permits reliance on another institution’s prior KYC without underlying
            documents. If not, budget for re-verification of 240k users or obtain
            the missing documents from Harbor’s records (if any exist outside the
            defunct vendor).\n3. **SAR review:** Do not attempt to review Harbor’s
            SARs pre-close without a legal mechanism (e.g., 314(b) agreement or regulatory
            approval). Instead, require Harbor to resolve the ~40 open alerts pre-close
            and provide representations regarding SAR filings.\n4. **Monitoring:**
            Validate the repoint of Harbor’s transaction feed to Mosaic’s engine in
            a test environment before close. Do not go live on day 1 without a parallel
            run period.\n---\n## Remaining gaps\n- **State-specific MTL transfer statutes:**
            The retrieved sources confirm state primacy in money transmission regulation
            [source:SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25] but do not provide the specific statutory
            text for the four new states or the 44 combined states. Exact state-by-state
            transfer/change-of-control requirements must be pulled from individual
            state statutes (e.g., California Money Transmission Act, New York Banking
            Law § 641).\n- **FinCEN CIP reliance guidance:** While the BSA requires
            recordkeeping sufficient to reconstruct transactions [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea],
            the specific FinCEN guidance on reliance on another MSB’s CIP (31 C.F.R.
            § 1010.100(ff)) was not retrieved. This guidance is necessary to confirm
            whether pass/fail results are ever sufficient.\n- **SAR confidentiality
            in M&A:** The retrieved sources confirm SAR confidentiality [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8]
            but do not provide the specific FinCEN guidance on SAR sharing in acquisitions
            (e.g., FIN-2018-G003 or similar).\n- **Bonus structure:** The structure
            of the $50 bonus (cash, credit, fee waiver) is unknown [Q-BONUS], preventing
            a definitive consumer-protection analysis.\n\n## Sources surfaced\n\n-
            Retrieved external authority: [The Bank Secrecy Act | FinCEN.gov](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/bank-secrecy-act)

              text: '**Likely answer:** Yes — this is not just a data migration. All
                four workstreams require legal review before the Nov 15 close, and
                the current plan contains at least one likely deal-blocker: the assumption
                that Harbor’s state money transmitter licenses (MTLs) can simply be
                "used" or "assumed" in an asset purchase. State MTLs are generally
                non-transferable; an asset purchase typically requires the buyer to
                obtain new licenses or specific state regulatory approval for a change
                of control, which is unlikely to be completed in 10 weeks. Additionally,
                the BSA/AML reliance plan fails because Mosaic Relay cannot satisfy
                its own Customer Identification Program (CIP) obligations with pass/fail
                results alone when the underlying identity documents are missing,
                and the day-1 migration plan creates a transaction-monitoring gap
                that violates the requirement for continuous suspicious activity monitoring.

                **Conditional alternative:** If the deal were restructured as a stock
                purchase (or if Mosaic Relay already held licenses in the four "new"
                states), the licensing timeline risk would drop significantly, though
                the BSA/AML recordkeeping and SAR confidentiality issues would remain.

                ---

                ## Matter summary

                Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay in an asset purchase targeted
                to close Nov 15 (~10 weeks out). The plan involves migrating 240,000
                consumer and 12,000 business accounts into Mosaic’s app on day 1,
                relying on Harbor’s prior KYC (for which underlying documents are
                missing for pre-2023 users), assuming Harbor’s 38 state MTLs to create
                a combined 44-state footprint, and launching a $50 welcome bonus campaign.
                Harbor has ~40 open alerts and unreviewed SARs, and its transaction-monitoring
                SaaS contract terminates at close.

                ## Decision question

                Can Mosaic Relay proceed with the Nov 15 close and day-1 migration
                given that state MTLs are likely non-transferable in an asset purchase,
                CIP reliance on Harbor’s KYC is unsupported without underlying documents,
                and the monitoring/SAR review process is incomplete?

                ---

                ## Likely rules and issues

                ### 1. State money-transmitter licensing and transfer in an asset
                purchase

                **Federal vs. State:** Money transmission is regulated primarily at
                the state level; there is no federal money transmitter license. State
                financial regulators are the primary regulators of nonbanks operating
                within the United States [source:SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25].

                **The transfer problem:** State MTLs are generally non-transferable.
                In an asset purchase, the buyer (Mosaic Relay) must typically apply
                for new licenses or obtain explicit state approval for a change of
                control or license assumption. The plan to "use/assume Harbor''s licenses"
                for the four new markets [the internal record] is not viable without
                state-by-state regulatory approval. With close targeted in ~10 weeks,
                obtaining new MTLs or change-of-control approvals in 44 states is
                likely impossible; many states require 3–6 months or longer for new
                license applications.

                **Asset vs. stock distinction:** The acquisition is structured as
                an asset purchase [the internal record]. This structure exacerbates
                the licensing problem because licenses do not automatically transfer
                with assets. A stock purchase (or merger) might preserve the corporate
                entity holding the licenses, but an asset purchase requires affirmative
                regulatory approval for license transfer or new issuance.

                ### 2. BSA/AML and reliance on prior customer identification (CIP)

                **Federal requirement:** The Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) requires financial
                institutions to maintain records sufficient to enable transactions
                and activity in customer accounts to be reconstructed [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea].
                This includes implementing a Customer Identification Program (CIP)
                with risk-based procedures for verifying customer identity.

                **The reliance gap:** Mosaic Relay cannot simply rely on Harbor’s
                prior KYC pass/fail results. While FinCEN guidance permits reliance
                on another financial institution’s CIP in limited circumstances (e.g.,
                when the customer is opening a new account and the other institution
                provides specific certifications), that reliance requires the relying
                institution to obtain the underlying identity documentation or ensure
                the other institution retains it. Here, the underlying documents for
                pre-2023 users are missing [the internal record], and Harbor’s KYC
                vendor has shut down. Pass/fail results alone do not satisfy Mosaic
                Relay’s independent obligation to maintain records sufficient to reconstruct
                customer activity [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea].

                **Timing:** Mosaic Relay must perform its own CIP on day 1 when these
                customers open accounts with Mosaic. The "no re-verification" plan
                [the internal record] violates this requirement unless Mosaic can
                obtain the underlying documentation before migration.

                ### 3. Open alerts, SAR confidentiality, and transaction-monitoring
                continuity

                **SAR confidentiality:** SARs and any information that would reveal
                the existence of a SAR are confidential [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8].
                Unauthorized disclosure is prohibited. In an asset purchase, the buyer
                does not automatically acquire the right to review the seller’s SARs.
                Mosaic Relay cannot "read" Harbor’s SARs as part of diligence without
                violating confidentiality rules unless specific safe harbors apply
                (e.g., certain information sharing under Section 314(b), if both are
                participants, or through a FinCEN-approved process). The ~40 open
                alerts and "handful" of SARs [the internal record] represent unknown
                BSA/AML liability that Mosaic would assume upon migration.

                **Monitoring continuity:** The BSA requires financial institutions
                to report suspicious activity and maintain effective monitoring [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8].
                Harbor’s monitoring SaaS terminates at close [the internal record].
                Repointing the transaction feed to Mosaic’s engine on day 1 creates
                a high risk of a monitoring gap. If the repoint fails or is not validated,
                Mosaic will be operating 252,000 accounts without adequate suspicious
                activity monitoring, creating immediate BSA liability.

                ### 4. Consumer-protection requirements for the $50 first-transfer
                bonus

                **Federal:** The bonus likely triggers Regulation E (Electronic Fund
                Transfer Act) disclosure requirements if it involves electronic fund
                transfers, and potentially Regulation DD (Truth in Savings) if the
                account is a "savings" or "interest-bearing" account. The CFPB has
                taken enforcement action against deceptive bonus offers that fail
                to disclose material terms (e.g., minimum transfer amounts, time limits,
                or fees).

                **State:** State money transmitter laws and consumer protection statutes
                (UDAP) apply. Some states regulate promotional offers tied to money
                transmission. The bonus structure [Q-BONUS, left open] determines
                whether it constitutes a "gift" or "premium" subject to specific state
                banking or money transmitter regulations.

                ---

                ## Viable paths

                **Path A: Delay close (recommended candidate)**

                Postpone the close until Mosaic Relay can (1) obtain necessary state
                MTL approvals or licenses for the four new markets, (2) complete CIP
                re-verification or obtain missing KYC documents, (3) review the open
                alerts and SARs through a legally compliant process (e.g., 314(b)
                information sharing or post-close lookback), and (4) validate the
                monitoring repoint in a test environment. This preserves the deal
                but pushes the timeline.

                **Path B: Restructure as stock purchase**

                Convert the acquisition to a stock purchase or merger, allowing Harbor
                to retain its corporate existence and licenses (subject to change-of-control
                approvals, which are typically faster than new license applications).
                This does not solve the CIP documentation gap or SAR confidentiality
                issues but preserves the licensing footprint.

                **Path C: Close with phased migration (high risk)**

                Close on Nov 15 but delay the day-1 migration. Keep Harbor as a separate
                licensed entity operating under its own MTLs and monitoring until
                Mosaic obtains its own licenses and completes CIP. This requires maintaining
                Harbor’s infrastructure and compliance program post-close, which may
                be operationally difficult but avoids immediate unlicensed money transmission.

                ---

                ## Facts that could change the answer

                - **Deal structure:** If this were a stock purchase rather than an
                asset purchase [the internal record], the licensing analysis changes
                significantly (licenses stay with the entity, subject to change-of-control
                notice).

                - **CIP reliance program:** If Mosaic Relay’s AML/CIP program explicitly
                permits reliance on Harbor’s KYC under 31 C.F.R. § 1020.220(a)(6)
                (or equivalent MSB provision) and Harbor can provide the required
                certifications and access to underlying documents (even if not currently
                held), the no-reverification plan might be viable. Currently, this
                is unknown [the internal record].

                - **Bonus structure:** If the $50 bonus is structured as a credit
                to a stored-value account rather than a cash transfer, different consumer
                protection rules apply.

                ---

                ## Recommended last-mile verification

                1. **State licensing:** Immediately engage counsel in the four "new"
                states to confirm whether Harbor’s licenses can be transferred in
                an asset purchase or whether new applications are required. Do not
                assume the licenses are portable.

                2. **CIP compliance:** Have compliance confirm whether Mosaic’s CIP
                program permits reliance on another institution’s prior KYC without
                underlying documents. If not, budget for re-verification of 240k users
                or obtain the missing documents from Harbor’s records (if any exist
                outside the defunct vendor).

                3. **SAR review:** Do not attempt to review Harbor’s SARs pre-close
                without a legal mechanism (e.g., 314(b) agreement or regulatory approval).
                Instead, require Harbor to resolve the ~40 open alerts pre-close and
                provide representations regarding SAR filings.

                4. **Monitoring:** Validate the repoint of Harbor’s transaction feed
                to Mosaic’s engine in a test environment before close. Do not go live
                on day 1 without a parallel run period.

                ---

                ## Remaining gaps

                - **State-specific MTL transfer statutes:** The retrieved sources
                confirm state primacy in money transmission regulation [source:SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25]
                but do not provide the specific statutory text for the four new states
                or the 44 combined states. Exact state-by-state transfer/change-of-control
                requirements must be pulled from individual state statutes (e.g.,
                California Money Transmission Act, New York Banking Law § 641).

                - **FinCEN CIP reliance guidance:** While the BSA requires recordkeeping
                sufficient to reconstruct transactions [source:SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea],
                the specific FinCEN guidance on reliance on another MSB’s CIP (31
                C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)) was not retrieved. This guidance is necessary
                to confirm whether pass/fail results are ever sufficient.

                - **SAR confidentiality in M&A:** The retrieved sources confirm SAR
                confidentiality [source:SRC-af5274560289d39360e8] but do not provide
                the specific FinCEN guidance on SAR sharing in acquisitions (e.g.,
                FIN-2018-G003 or similar).

                - **Bonus structure:** The structure of the $50 bonus (cash, credit,
                fee waiver) is unknown [Q-BONUS], preventing a definitive consumer-protection
                analysis.'

                available_excerpt: "CONFERENCE OF STATE BANK SUPERVISORS\n\n# REENGINEERING
                  NONBANK\n\n# SUPERVISION\n\n## Chapter Four: Overview of Money Services
                  Business\n\n### October 2019\n\n---\n\nAbout This Paper\n\nThis
                  paper, Reengineering Nonbank Supervision, serves two primary purposes.
                  First, as a stakeholder\nawareness document covering state supervision
                  of the nonbank marketplace, and second, as a change \ndocument or
                  roadmap to assist state supervisors in identifying the current state
                  of supervision and\nmaking informed changes to state supervisory
                  processes. The paper is comprised of several standalone \nchapters
                  that together will cover the industry supervised by state nonbank
                  financial regulators, the \nexisting system of supervision for nonbanks
                  and the challenges and opportunities for state supervisors\nin “reengineering”
                  that system.\n\nThe chapters provide a broad overview of the industry
                  participants and how they are regulated by state\nnonbank supervisors.
                  We combine these sometimes unlike participants into a single industry
                  of\nnonbanks due more to jurisdictional coverage and supervisory
                  constructs than similarities between the\nparticipants themselves.
                  The common theme is that all of these participants provide or facilitate
                  \nconsumer products and services and fall under the authorities
                  granted to nonbank supervisors.\n\nState financial regulators are
                  the primary regulators of nonbanks operating within the United States.
                  \nTogether, they have forged a series of initiatives, collectively
                  known as CSBS Vision 2020, to modernize \nnonbank licensing and
                  supervision. This paper contributes research and engages discussion
                  on possible \nactions that might be taken.\n\nChapters to Date\n\nChapter
                  1 – Introduction to the Nonbank Industry\nChapter 2 – Overview of
                  State Nonbank Supervision\n\nAcknowledgements\n\nThe paper is staff-developed
                  under the direction of the CSBS Non-Depository Supervisory Committee.
                  In \ncreating this paper, we have interviewed over 80 subject matter
                  experts from industry and state \ngovernment. Ackno"

                available_excerpt: 'BANK SECRECY ACT, ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING,

                  AND OFFICE OF FOREIGN ASSETS CONTROL


                  Section 8.1


                  INTRODUCTION TO THE BANK

                  SECRECY ACT


                  The Financial Recordkeeping and Reporting of Currency

                  and Foreign Transactions Act of 1970 (31 U.S.C. 5311 et seq.) is
                  referred to as the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). The purpose of the BSA
                  is to require United States (U.S.)

                  financial institutions to maintain appropriate records and file
                  certain reports involving currency (transactions and a financial
                  institution''s customer relationships. Currency

                  Transactions Reports (CTRs) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs)
                  are the primary means used by banks to satisfy the requirements
                  of the BSA. The recordkeeping regulations also include the requirement
                  that a financial institution''s records be sufficient to enable
                  transactions and activity in customer accounts to be reconstructed
                  if necessary. In doing so, a paper and audit trail is maintained.
                  These records and reports have a high degree of usefulness in criminal,
                  tax, or regulatory investigations or proceedings.


                  The BSA consists of two parts: Title I Financial Recordkeeping and
                  Title II Reports of Currency and Foreign Transactions. Title I authorizes
                  the Secretary of the Department of the Treasury (Treasury) to issue
                  regulations, which required insured financial institutions to maintain
                  certain records. Title II directed the Treasury to prescribe regulations
                  governing the reporting of certain transactions by and through financial
                  institutions in excess of $10,000 in each currency transaction over
                  $10,000. A currency transaction is any transaction involving the
                  physical transfer of currency from one person to another and covers
                  deposits, withdrawals, exchanges, or transfers of currency or other
                  payments. Currency is defined as currency and coin of the U.S. or
                  any other country as long as it is customarily accepted as money
                  in the country of issue.


                  The implementing regulations under the BSA were originally intended
                  to aid investigations into an arr'

                  # The Bank Secrecy Act


                  The Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act of 1970, its
                  amendments, and the other statutes relating to the subject matter
                  of that Act, have come to be referred to as the Bank Secrecy Act
                  (BSA). The BSA authorizes the Department of the Treasury to impose
                  reporting and other requirements on financial institutions and other
                  businesses to help detect and prevent money laundering. Specifically,
                  the regulations implementing the BSA require financial institutions
                  to, among other things, keep records of cash purchases of negotiable
                  instruments, file reports of cash transactions exceeding $10,000
                  (daily aggregate amount), and to report suspicious activity that
                  might signify money laundering, tax evasion, or other criminal activities.
                  The BSA is sometimes referred to as an "anti-money laundering" (AML)
                  law or jointly as “BSA/AML,” and is codified at 12 U.S.C. 1829b,
                  12 U.S.C. 1951-1960, 31 U.S.C. 5311-5314, 5316-5336, and includes
                  notes thereto.

                available_excerpt: "CONFERENCE OF STATE BANK SUPERVISORS\n\n# REENGINEERING
                  NONBANK\n\n# SUPERVISION\n\n## Chapter Four: Overview of Money Services
                  Business\n\n### October 2019\n\n---\n\nAbout This Paper\n\nThis
                  paper, Reengineering Nonbank Supervision, serves two primary purposes.
                  First, as a stakeholder\nawareness document covering state supervision
                  of the nonbank marketplace, and second, as a change \ndocument or
                  roadmap to assist state supervisors in identifying the current state
                  of supervision and\nmaking informed changes to state supervisory
                  processes. The paper is comprised of several standalone \nchapters
                  that together will cover the industry supervised by state nonbank
                  financial regulators, the \nexisting system of supervision for nonbanks
                  and the challenges and opportunities for state supervisors\nin “reengineering”
                  that system.\n\nThe chapters provide a broad overview of the industry
                  participants and how they are regulated by state\nnonbank supervisors.
                  We combine these sometimes unlike participants into a single industry
                  of\nnonbanks due more to jurisdictional coverage and supervisory
                  constructs than similarities between the\nparticipants themselves.
                  The common theme is that all of these participants provide or facilitate
                  \nconsumer products and services and fall under the authorities
                  granted to nonbank supervisors.\n\nState financial regulators are
                  the primary regulators of nonbanks operating within the United States.
                  \nTogether, they have forged a series of initiatives, collectively
                  known as CSBS Vision 2020, to modernize \nnonbank licensing and
                  supervision. This paper contributes research and engages discussion
                  on possible \nactions that might be taken.\n\nChapters to Date\n\nChapter
                  1 – Introduction to the Nonbank Industry\nChapter 2 – Overview of
                  State Nonbank Supervision\n\nAcknowledgements\n\nThe paper is staff-developed
                  under the direction of the CSBS Non-Depository Supervisory Committee.
                  In \ncreating this paper, we have interviewed over 80 subject matter
                  experts from industry and state \ngovernment. Ackno"

                source_id: SRC-23325868d05d711df7ea
                available_excerpt: 'BANK SECRECY ACT, ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING,

                  AND OFFICE OF FOREIGN ASSETS CONTROL


                  Section 8.1


                  INTRODUCTION TO THE BANK

                  SECRECY ACT


                  The Financial Recordkeeping and Reporting of Currency

                  and Foreign Transactions Act of 1970 (31 U.S.C. 5311 et seq.) is
                  referred to as the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). The purpose of the BSA
                  is to require United States (U.S.)

                  financial institutions to maintain appropriate records and file
                  certain reports involving currency (transactions and a financial
                  institution''s customer relationships. Currency

                  Transactions Reports (CTRs) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs)
                  are the primary means used by banks to satisfy the requirements
                  of the BSA. The recordkeeping regulations also include the requirement
                  that a financial institution''s records be sufficient to enable
                  transactions and activity in customer accounts to be reconstructed
                  if necessary. In doing so, a paper and audit trail is maintained.
                  These records and reports have a high degree of usefulness in criminal,
                  tax, or regulatory investigations or proceedings.


                  The BSA consists of two parts: Title I Financial Recordkeeping and
                  Title II Reports of Currency and Foreign Transactions. Title I authorizes
                  the Secretary of the Department of the Treasury (Treasury) to issue
                  regulations, which required insured financial institutions to maintain
                  certain records. Title II directed the Treasury to prescribe regulations
                  governing the reporting of certain transactions by and through financial
                  institutions in excess of $10,000 in each currency transaction over
                  $10,000. A currency transaction is any transaction involving the
                  physical transfer of currency from one person to another and covers
                  deposits, withdrawals, exchanges, or transfers of currency or other
                  payments. Currency is defined as currency and coin of the U.S. or
                  any other country as long as it is customarily accepted as money
                  in the country of issue.

                  to aid investigations into an arr'

                # The Bank Secrecy Act


                The Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act of 1970, its amendments,
                and the other statutes relating to the subject matter of that Act,
                have come to be referred to as the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). The BSA
                authorizes the Department of the Treasury to impose reporting and
                other requirements on financial institutions and other businesses
                to help detect and prevent money laundering. Specifically, the regulations
                implementing the BSA require financial institutions to, among other
                things, keep records of cash purchases of negotiable instruments,
                file reports of cash transactions exceeding $10,000 (daily aggregate
                amount), and to report suspicious activity that might signify money
                laundering, tax evasion, or other criminal activities. The BSA is
                sometimes referred to as an "anti-money laundering" (AML) law or jointly
                as “BSA/AML,” and is codified at 12 U.S.C. 1829b, 12 U.S.C. 1951-1960,

            - source_id: SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25
              source_label: '[PDF] REENGINEERING NONBANK SUPERVISION - CSBS'
              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-00e489d1e0295d2fad25-d05b07e64729.md
              url: https://www.csbs.org/chapter-four-overview-of-money-service-business
              available_excerpt: "CONFERENCE OF STATE BANK SUPERVISORS\n\n# REENGINEERING
                NONBANK\n\n# SUPERVISION\n\n## Chapter Four: Overview of Money Services
                Business\n\n### October 2019\n\n---\n\nAbout This Paper\n\nThis paper,
                Reengineering Nonbank Supervision, serves two primary purposes. First,
                as a stakeholder\nawareness document covering state supervision of
                the nonbank marketplace, and second, as a change \ndocument or roadmap
                to assist state supervisors in identifying the current state of supervision
                and\nmaking informed changes to state supervisory processes. The paper
                is comprised of several standalone \nchapters that together will cover
                the industry supervised by state nonbank financial regulators, the
                \nexisting system of supervision for nonbanks and the challenges and
                opportunities for state supervisors\nin “reengineering” that system.\n\nThe
                chapters provide a broad overview of the industry participants and
                how they are regulated by state\nnonbank supervisors. We combine these
                sometimes unlike participants into a single industry of\nnonbanks
                due more to jurisdictional coverage and supervisory constructs than
                similarities between the\nparticipants themselves. The common theme
                is that all of these participants provide or facilitate \nconsumer
                products and services and fall under the authorities granted to nonbank
                supervisors.\n\nState financial regulators are the primary regulators
                of nonbanks operating within the United States. \nTogether, they have
                forged a series of initiatives, collectively known as CSBS Vision
                2020, to modernize \nnonbank licensing and supervision. This paper
                contributes research and engages discussion on possible \nactions
                that might be taken.\n\nChapters to Date\n\nChapter 1 – Introduction
                to the Nonbank Industry\nChapter 2 – Overview of State Nonbank Supervision\n\nAcknowledgements\n\nThe
                paper is staff-developed under the direction of the CSBS Non-Depository
                Supervisory Committee. In \ncreating this paper, we have interviewed
                over 80 subject matter experts from industry and state \ngovernment.
                Ackno"

              available_excerpt: 'BANK SECRECY ACT, ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING,

                AND OFFICE OF FOREIGN ASSETS CONTROL


                Section 8.1


                INTRODUCTION TO THE BANK

                SECRECY ACT


                The Financial Recordkeeping and Reporting of Currency

                and Foreign Transactions Act of 1970 (31 U.S.C. 5311 et seq.) is referred
                to as the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). The purpose of the BSA is to require
                United States (U.S.)

                financial institutions to maintain appropriate records and file certain
                reports involving currency (transactions and a financial institution''s
                customer relationships. Currency

                Transactions Reports (CTRs) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs)
                are the primary means used by banks to satisfy the requirements of
                the BSA. The recordkeeping regulations also include the requirement
                that a financial institution''s records be sufficient to enable transactions
                and activity in customer accounts to be reconstructed if necessary.
                In doing so, a paper and audit trail is maintained. These records
                and reports have a high degree of usefulness in criminal, tax, or
                regulatory investigations or proceedings.


                The BSA consists of two parts: Title I Financial Recordkeeping and
                Title II Reports of Currency and Foreign Transactions. Title I authorizes
                the Secretary of the Department of the Treasury (Treasury) to issue
                regulations, which required insured financial institutions to maintain
                certain records. Title II directed the Treasury to prescribe regulations
                governing the reporting of certain transactions by and through financial
                institutions in excess of $10,000 in each currency transaction over
                $10,000. A currency transaction is any transaction involving the physical
                transfer of currency from one person to another and covers deposits,
                withdrawals, exchanges, or transfers of currency or other payments.
                Currency is defined as currency and coin of the U.S. or any other
                country as long as it is customarily accepted as money in the country
                of issue.


                The implementing regulations under the BSA were originally intended
                to aid investigations into an arr'

          remain: # Research whether a money transmitter license can transfer or remain


          ## Questi…'
        source_class: saved_artifact
        path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md
        available_excerpt: "# Research whether a money transmitter license can transfer
          or remain\n\n## Question\n\nResearch whether a money transmitter license
          can transfer or remain usable after an asset acquisition, including state
          notice, approval, interim-operation, and partner-bank custody issues.\n\n##
          Working Analysis\n\n## Practical answer\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
          transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
          Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated
          launch by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close.
          However, Mosaic should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only
          states unless one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its own
          license.\n2. The state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3.
          The regulator confirms a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains the
          real licensed provider under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks
          regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account
          is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service
          provider. If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses
          alive might not give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified operative
          authority retrieved.** The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission
          Modernization Act and a New York regulator licensing page. However, no exact
          provision about an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation, or custody
          was available for review. Also, a model act is not proof of the law adopted
          in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions below remain conditional.\n\n##
          Work needed before launch\n\n| Work | Why | Proposed owner | Needed by |
          Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Identify
          the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest authority gap
          | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered activities |
          Block regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix for every
          affected state | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules can differ
          | State regulatory counsel | Before the closing conditions are final | Applicable
          rule, filing deadline, regulator response, and license status | Delay migration
          in the affected state |\n| Confirm the post-close service provider | The
          licensed entity must match the actual operating model | Product and deal
          counsel | Before customer notices and account design are final | Contracts,
          user interface, funds-flow diagram, and operating roles | Keep Harbor as
          the actual provider where permitted |\n| Review notices and approvals |
          An asset sale can create separate seller and buyer requirements | Licensing
          team | Before each state deadline | Filing receipts and required approvals
          or non-objections | Make approval a state launch condition |\n| Confirm
          interim operating authority | A pending application should not be assumed
          to permit operation | State regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable
          rule or written regulator confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated
          or restrict transactions |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody
          does not, by itself, establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel
          and bank relationship owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account
          titles, control rights, reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds
          and obligations in the existing structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and
          surrender plans | Harbor may retain duties for balances, claims, records,
          and reports | Harbor compliance and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational
          shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and continued bonds and financial coverage
          | Keep Harbor licensed and operational longer |\n\n## State notice and approval\n\nDo
          not search only for a rule called “license transfer.” Review each state
          for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n- change of control;\n- change
          in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n- assignment of outstanding
          payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons, locations, or agents;\n-
          license surrender or termination;\n- customer agreement assignment; and\n-
          movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn asset purchase might
          fall outside a technical “change of control” rule because Harbor’s ownership
          does not change. That does not resolve the issue. Harbor might still need
          a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic might separately need authority before
          it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe state matrix should distinguish:\n\n-
          notice only;\n- approval before closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n-
          new license required;\n- operation permitted while an application is pending;\n-
          regulator-approved transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n##
          Interim operation\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition
          period. However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA
          supportable structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains
          responsible to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n-
          Harbor controls the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses,
          bonds, and financial coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding
          obligations remain covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints,
          and examinations.\n- Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational
          role is permitted.\n- The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each relevant
          regulator permits or accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan creates
          tension with this approach. A single Mosaic account, one combined balance,
          and full access to Mosaic products make it harder to show that Harbor remains
          the true provider.\n\n## Partner-bank custody\n\nA partner bank account
          is not automatically a substitute for a money transmitter license. The key
          questions concern the complete activity and obligation flow.\n\nFor each
          customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives the customer’s
          instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit or return the funds?\n3.
          In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is it a custodial or “for benefit
          of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6. Who owns the ledger and
          resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer fails?\n8. Which entity
          owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s license, bond, and permissible
          investments cover the obligation?\n10. Does the bank agreement permit assignment,
          migration, or a change in the program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required
          before closing or migration?\n12. What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic,
          or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA bank-led model might provide a different
          licensing analysis if the bank is the actual provider and Mosaic performs
          only permitted services. A bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic
          or Harbor is different. The legal documents, customer terms, control rights,
          and actual operations must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n-
          account segregation;\n- daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve
          funding;\n- bank setoff rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n- continuity
          if the account is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return and
          chargeback duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n-
          whether any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual account
          structure.\n\n## Recommended closing position\n\nKeep the acquisition closing
          separate from the regulated-service launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only
          states, use a state launch hold unless Mosaic has documented authority.
          For overlapping states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing licenses cover the
          complete post-close product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s
          licenses or release its bonds until the applicable regulators permit it
          and all outstanding obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed
          into an approved run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change
          the current recommendation. It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody
          is part of the licensing analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority
          gap.**\n\n## Sources surfaced\n\n- Retrieved source: [PDF CSBS Money Transmission
          Modernization Act](https://www.csbs.org/sites/default/files/2023-02/CSBS%20Money%20Transmission%20Modernization%20Act.pdf)
          [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n  No relevant passage has been selected;
          open the source.\n- Retrieved source: [Money Transmitter Licensing | Department

          path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/RES-20260911-0a5f07.md
          name: RES-20260911-0a5f07.md
          content: "# Research whether a money transmitter license can transfer or
            remain\n\n## Question\n\nResearch whether a money transmitter license
            can transfer or remain usable after an asset acquisition, including state
            notice, approval, interim-operation, and partner-bank custody issues.\n\n##
            Working Analysis\n\n## Practical answer\n\n**Do not treat Harbor’s money
            transmitter licenses as assets that move to Mosaic in the asset purchase.**
            Use this closing rule:\n\n> **No confirmed authority means no regulated
            launch by Mosaic in that state.**\n\nThe asset purchase can still close.
            However, Mosaic should not activate regulated services in the four Harbor-only
            states unless one of these conditions is met:\n\n1. Mosaic obtains its
            own license.\n2. The state approves a transfer or other license change.\n3.
            The regulator confirms a lawful interim structure.\n4. Harbor remains
            the real licensed provider under a valid transition plan.\n5. Mosaic blocks
            regulated functions in that state.\n\nThe planned unified Mosaic account
            is important. It suggests that Mosaic, not Harbor, will become the service
            provider. If that is correct, keeping Harbor’s legal entity and licenses
            alive might not give Mosaic authority to operate.\n\n**No verified operative
            authority retrieved.** The collection found the CSBS Model Money Transmission
            Modernization Act and a New York regulator licensing page. However, no
            exact provision about an asset sale, license transfer, interim operation,
            or custody was available for review. Also, a model act is not proof of
            the law adopted in a specific state. The state-specific conclusions below
            remain conditional.\n\n## Work needed before launch\n\n| Work | Why |
            Proposed owner | Needed by | Evidence to proceed | Fallback |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n|
            Identify the four Harbor-only states | These states have the clearest
            authority gap | Licensing team | Now | Confirmed license list and covered
            activities | Block regulated functions in those states |\n| Build a matrix
            for every affected state | Transfer, notice, approval, and surrender rules
            can differ | State regulatory counsel | Before the closing conditions
            are final | Applicable rule, filing deadline, regulator response, and
            license status | Delay migration in the affected state |\n| Confirm the
            post-close service provider | The licensed entity must match the actual
            operating model | Product and deal counsel | Before customer notices and
            account design are final | Contracts, user interface, funds-flow diagram,
            and operating roles | Keep Harbor as the actual provider where permitted
            |\n| Review notices and approvals | An asset sale can create separate
            seller and buyer requirements | Licensing team | Before each state deadline
            | Filing receipts and required approvals or non-objections | Make approval
            a state launch condition |\n| Confirm interim operating authority | A
            pending application should not be assumed to permit operation | State
            regulatory counsel | Before close | Applicable rule or written regulator
            confirmation | Keep Harbor customers segregated or restrict transactions
            |\n| Review partner-bank arrangements | Bank custody does not, by itself,
            establish Mosaic’s licensing position | Payments counsel and bank relationship
            owner | Before balances move | Bank agreements, account titles, control
            rights, reconciliation design, and bank consent | Keep funds and obligations
            in the existing structure |\n| Prepare license run-off and surrender plans
            | Harbor may retain duties for balances, claims, records, and reports
            | Harbor compliance and deal counsel | Before surrender or operational
            shutdown | Regulator-approved plan and continued bonds and financial coverage
            | Keep Harbor licensed and operational longer |\n\n## State notice and
            approval\n\nDo not search only for a rule called “license transfer.” Review
            each state for:\n\n- sale of substantially all assets;\n- change of control;\n-
            change in business plan;\n- change in licensed activities;\n- assignment
            of outstanding payment obligations;\n- change in responsible persons,
            locations, or agents;\n- license surrender or termination;\n- customer
            agreement assignment; and\n- movement of stored balances or customer funds.\n\nAn
            asset purchase might fall outside a technical “change of control” rule
            because Harbor’s ownership does not change. That does not resolve the
            issue. Harbor might still need a notice or surrender approval. Mosaic
            might separately need authority before it starts the regulated activity.\n\nThe
            state matrix should distinguish:\n\n- notice only;\n- approval before
            closing;\n- approval before customer migration;\n- new license required;\n-
            operation permitted while an application is pending;\n- regulator-approved
            transition available; and\n- no supported interim path.\n\n## Interim
            operation\n\nHarbor could remain the licensed provider for a transition
            period. However, the structure must be real, not only contractual language.\n\nA
            supportable structure would normally need to show that:\n\n- Harbor remains
            responsible to customers.\n- Customer terms name Harbor as the provider.\n-
            Harbor controls the regulated activity as required.\n- Harbor’s licenses,
            bonds, and financial coverage remain active.\n- Customer funds and outstanding
            obligations remain covered.\n- Harbor can complete reports, refunds, complaints,
            and examinations.\n- Required records remain available.\n- Mosaic’s operational
            role is permitted.\n- The partner bank accepts the structure.\n- Each
            relevant regulator permits or accepts the structure.\n\nThe present plan
            creates tension with this approach. A single Mosaic account, one combined
            balance, and full access to Mosaic products make it harder to show that
            Harbor remains the true provider.\n\n## Partner-bank custody\n\nA partner
            bank account is not automatically a substitute for a money transmitter
            license. The key questions concern the complete activity and obligation
            flow.\n\nFor each customer balance and transfer, document:\n\n1. Who receives
            the customer’s instruction?\n2. Who accepts the obligation to transmit
            or return the funds?\n3. In whose name is the bank account held?\n4. Is
            it a custodial or “for benefit of” account?\n5. Who can direct withdrawals?\n6.
            Who owns the ledger and resolves errors?\n7. Who bears loss if a transfer
            fails?\n8. Which entity owes the customer a refund?\n9. Which entity’s
            license, bond, and permissible investments cover the obligation?\n10.
            Does the bank agreement permit assignment, migration, or a change in the
            program manager?\n11. Is bank consent required before closing or migration?\n12.
            What happens to funds if Harbor, Mosaic, or the bank relationship ends?\n\nA
            bank-led model might provide a different licensing analysis if the bank
            is the actual provider and Mosaic performs only permitted services. A
            bank account that merely holds funds for Mosaic or Harbor is different.
            The legal documents, customer terms, control rights, and actual operations
            must all support the claimed model.\n\nAlso review:\n\n- account segregation;\n-
            daily reconciliation;\n- shortfalls and reserve funding;\n- bank setoff
            rights;\n- liens and security interests;\n- continuity if the account
            is frozen;\n- treatment of pending transfers;\n- return and chargeback
            duties;\n- insolvency treatment;\n- customer disclosures; and\n- whether
            any deposit-insurance statement is accurate for the actual account structure.\n\n##
            Recommended closing position\n\nKeep the acquisition closing separate
            from the regulated-service launch.\n\nFor the four Harbor-only states,
            use a state launch hold unless Mosaic has documented authority. For overlapping
            states, confirm that Mosaic’s existing licenses cover the complete post-close
            product set and funds flow.\n\nDo not surrender Harbor’s licenses or release
            its bonds until the applicable regulators permit it and all outstanding
            obligations have been assigned, completed, or placed into an approved
            run-off structure.\n\nThis investigation does not change the current recommendation.
            It adds one material point: **partner-bank custody is part of the licensing
            analysis, but custody alone does not cure an authority gap.**\n\n## Sources
            surfaced\n\n- Retrieved source: [PDF CSBS Money Transmission Modernization
            Act](https://www.csbs.org/sites/default/files/2023-02/CSBS%20Money%20Transmission%20Modernization%20Act.pdf)
            [source:SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538]\n  No relevant passage has been selected;
            open the source.\n- Retrieved source: [Money Transmitter Licensing | Department
            of Financial Services](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/apps_and_licensing/money_transmitters)
            [source:SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4]\n  No relevant passage has been selected;
            open the source.\n- Retrieved source: [OCC Confirms National Bank Act
            Preempts State Money Transmitter ...](https://www.troutmanfinancialservices.com/2026/06/occ-confirms-national-bank-act-preempts-state-money-transmitter-licensing-for-fidelity-digital-assets/)
            [source:SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413]\n  No relevant passage has been selected;
            open the source.\n- Retrieved source: [How To Get A Money Transmitter
            License (MTL) in the U.S. - Fenergo](https://resources.fenergo.com/blogs/how-to-get-a-money-transmitter-license)
            [source:SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200]\n  No relevant passage has been selected;
            open the source.\n\n## Last-mile work for counsel\n\n- Confirm the facts
            that could change the recommendation.\n- Verify any authority that will
            carry the final answer.\n- Decide the acceptable risk and the business
            path.\n\n## Research status\n\n- Question answered: Yes\n- External authority
            retrieved: Yes\n- Internal support used: No\n- Model-only: No\n- Assumptions:
            See the Working Analysis.\n- Remaining gaps: Verify material facts and
            any authority used for the final answer.\n"
