                    body_hash: 2245b178c49fc1f157bf15c133c59f8fcfe9abdf43f0bf94df397229a7889584
                    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000004.md
                    text: "ly for goods or services provided by the issuer or its
                      affiliate or franchisees of the issuer \nor its affiliate, except
                      to the extent required by applicable law to be redeemable in
                      cash for its cash \nvalue; \n(f) \n\"Control\" means \n(1) \n(A)
                      the power to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 25 percent
                      of \nthe outstanding voting shares or voting interests of a
                      licensee or person in control of a \nlicensee; \n(B) \nthe power
                      to elect or appoint a majority of key individuals or \nexecutive
                      officers, managers, directors, trustees, or other persons exercising
                      \nmanagerial authority of a person in control of a licensee;
                      or \n(C) \nthe power to exercise, directly or indirectly, a
                      controlling \ninfluence over the management or policies of a
                      licensee or person in control of a \nlicensee. \n(2) \nRebuttable
                      Presumption of Control. \n(A) \nA person is presumed to exercise
                      a controlling influence \nwhen the person holds the power to
                      vote, directly or indirectly, at least 10 percent \nof the outstanding
                      voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person in
                      control \nof a licensee.2 \n(B) \nA person presumed to exercise
                      a controlling influence as \ndefined by this [Section 2.01(f)]
                      can rebut the presumption of control if the person \nis a passive
                      investor. \n(3) \nFor purposes of determining the percentage
                      of a person controlled \nby any other person, the person's interest
                      shall be aggregated with the interest of any other \nimmediate
                      family member, including the person's spouse, parents, children,
                      siblings, \nmothers- and fathers-in law, sons- and daughters-in-law,
                      brothers- and sisters-in-law, and \nany other person who shares
                      such person's home. \n(g) \n\"Eligible rating\" shall mean a
                      credit rating of any of the three highest rating \ncategories
                      provided by an eligible rating service, whereby each category
                      may include rating \n \n2 Commentary: The obligation to rebut
                      control rests exclusively with the person acquiring ≥10% of
                      the outstanding \nvoting shares or voting interests of a licensee
                      or person in control of a licensee.  It is not the responsibility
                      of the \nlicensee to rebut control.  This is consistent with
                      Section 601(a) of the Act which requires the person acquiring
                      control \nto obtain prior approval.\n"

                    text: "30 \n \n(1) \nappoint the person signing the contract as
                      the licensee's authorized \ndelegate with the authority to conduct
                      money transmission on behalf of the licensee; \n(2) \nset forth
                      the nature and scope of the relationship between the \nlicensee
                      and the authorized delegate and the respective rights and responsibilities
                      of the \nparties; \n(3) \nrequire the authorized delegate to
                      agree to fully comply with all \napplicable state and federal
                      laws, rules, and regulations pertaining to money transmission,
                      \nincluding this [Act] and regulations implementing this [Act],
                      relevant provisions of the \nBank Secrecy Act and the USA PATRIOT
                      ACT; \n(4) \nrequire the authorized delegate to remit and handle
                      money and \nmonetary value in accordance with the terms of the
                      contract between the licensee and the \nauthorized delegate;
                      \n(5) \nimpose a trust on money and monetary value net of fees
                      received for \nmoney transmission for the benefit of the licensee;
                      \n(6) \nrequire the authorized delegate to prepare and maintain
                      records as \nrequired by this [Act] or regulations implementing
                      this [Act], or as reasonably requested \nby the [Commissioner];
                      \n(7) \nacknowledge that the authorized delegate consents to
                      examination \nor investigation by the [Commissioner]; \n(8)
                      \nstate that the licensee is subject to regulation by the [Commissioner]
                      \nand that, as part of that regulation, the [Commissioner] may
                      suspend or revoke an \nauthorized delegate designation or require
                      the licensee to terminate an authorized delegate \ndesignation;
                      and \n(9) \n(9)  acknowledge receipt of the written policies
                      and procedures \nrequired under [Section 8.01(b)(1)]. \n(e)
                      \nIf the licensee's license is suspended, revoked, surrendered,
                      or expired, the \nlicensee must, within five (5) business days,
                      provide documentation to the [Commissioner] that \nthe licensee
                      has notified all applicable authorized delegates of the licensee
                      whose names are in a \nrecord filed with the [Commissioner]
                      of the suspension, revocation, surrender, or expiration of a
                      \nlicense. Upon suspension, revocation, surrender, or expiration
                      of a license, applicable authorized \ndelegates shall immediately
                      cease to provide money transmission as an authorized delegate
                      of the \nlicensee. \n(f) \nAn authorized delegate of a licensee
                      holds in trust for the benefit of the \nlicensee all money net
                      of fees received from money transmission.  If any authorized
                      delegate \ncommingles any funds received from money transmission
                      with any other funds or property owned \nor controlled by the
                      authorized delegate, all commingled funds and other property
                      shall be \nconsidered held in trust in favor of the licensee
                      in an amount equal to the amount of money net of\n"

                    unit_id: p000031
                    start: 0
                    end: 2704

                    body_hash: 994d5382d8c2640923eca8c8aabbca98c8fbaeec037edafbf7675c1a3819b1e7
                    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000031.md
                    text: "31 \n \nfees received from money transmission.22 \n(g)
                      \nAn authorized delegate may not use a subdelegate to conduct
                      money \ntransmission on behalf of a licensee. \nSection 8.02
                      Unauthorized Activities \nA person shall not engage in the business
                      of money transmission on behalf of a person \nnot licensed under
                      this [Act]  or not exempt pursuant to [Article III] of this
                      [Act]. A person that \nengages in such activity provides money
                      transmission to the same extent as if the person were a \nlicensee,
                      and shall be jointly and severally liable with the unlicensed
                      or nonexempt person. \nSection 8.03 [Optional]: Prohibited Authorized
                      Delegates. \n(a) \nThe [appropriate court] in an action brought
                      by a licensee shall have \njurisdiction to grant appropriate
                      equitable or legal relief, including without limitation prohibiting
                      \nthe authorized delegate from directly or indirectly acting
                      as an authorized delegate for any licensee \nin this state and
                      the payment of restitution, damages or other monetary relief,
                      if the [appropriate \ncourt] finds that an authorized delegate
                      failed to remit money in accordance with the written \ncontract
                      required by [Section 8.01(b)] or as otherwise directed by the
                      licensee or required by law. \n(b) \nIf the [appropriate court]
                      issues an order prohibiting a person from acting as \nan authorized
                      delegate for any licensee pursuant to [Section 8.03(a)], the
                      licensee that brought the \naction shall report the order to
                      the [Commissioner] within thirty (30) days and shall report
                      the \norder through NMLS within ninety (90) days. \n(c) \nAn
                      authorized delegate who holds money in trust for the benefit
                      of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails to remit more than [$XXX]
                      of such money is guilty of a [reference \nto state classification]
                      felony. \n(d) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money in trust
                      for the benefit of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails to remit
                      no more than [$XXX] of such money is guilty of a [reference
                      \nto state classification] misdemeanor. \nARTICLE IX  \nTimely
                      Transmission, Refunds, and Disclosures \nSection 9.01 Timely
                      Transmission. \n(a) \nEvery licensee shall forward all money
                      received for transmission in \naccordance with the terms of
                      the agreement between the licensee and the sender unless the
                      licensee \nhas a reasonable belief or a reasonable basis to
                      believe that the sender may be a victim of fraud or \nthat a
                      crime or violation of law, rule, or regulation has occurred,
                      is occurring, or may occur. \n(b) \nIf a licensee fails to forward
                      money received for transmission in accordance \nwith this section,
                      the licensee must respond to inquiries by the sender with the
                      reason for the failure \n \n22 Commentary: An express trust
                      account or segregated bank account is not required.\n"

                    path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4/d021ece0cde82565eb83511c8122c85b/sections/s000001.md
                    text: 'ey Transmitter License.


                      Access to NMLS


                      NMLS is a secure web-based system created by state regulators
                      to provide efficiencies in the processing of state licenses
                      and improve supervision of state-regulated industries.


                      To access NMLS for the first time, you must complete a Company
                      Account Request Form and identify a Primary Account Administrator
                      and a Secondary Account Administrator. This form can be submitted
                      online through the NMLS website in the Getting Started section.
                      This form needs to be submitted only once per company, regardless
                      of the number of NMLS participating states in which you are
                      licensed.


                      Within three days of completing and submitting the Company Account
                      Request Form, the Primary Account Administrator will receive
                      NMLS login information. The Primary Account Administrator will
                      have full rights to access the system, submit information to
                      this agency and other participating state regulators, and set
                      up other company users in the system. Instructions and tutorials
                      on how to access and use the system are also available in the
                      NMLS Resource Center .


                      Note : If your company already has a record in NMLS, you can
                      omit this step.


                      Managing Your License on NMLS


                      Each company holding a DFS Money Transmitter License who wishes
                      to manage their license on NMLS must create a company record
                      in the system. To gain access to NMLS, the applicant must submit
                      a form requesting an NMLS account.


                      Current New York State Money Transmitters may transition their
                      licenses to NMLS. See the DFS Money Transmitter Transition Checklist
                      for more information.


                      Submitting a Complete Application


                      To submit an application and ensure your application is received,
                      acknowledged as complete, and processed, please follow the instructions
                      on the DFS Money Transmitter Checklists . No application shall
                      be deemed to be complete until the Department has received all
                      required information, documents, and fees.


                      In the process of reviewing and considering the application,
                      DFS may request additional information and supporting documents.


                      In the application process, an NMLS Identification Number will
                      be assigned to your application. Please maintain a record of
                      this NMLS Identification Number, as it will be used as your
                      application reference number throughout the remainder of the
                      application process. The applicant’s NMLS Identification Number
                      must be included on every hard-copy document submitted to the
                      Department.


                      Note : If the applicant has already submitted Forms MU1 and
                      MU2 through NMLS for another state, the applicant does not need
                      to re-enter the company record into NMLS. However, the applicant
                      is required to provide jurisdiction-specific information to
                      support its New York State application.


                      Back to Top ▲


                      Next Section


                      Continue


                      Annual Reporting


                      The Annual Report should be prepared by qualified persons and
                      submitted within 120 days following the close of the calendar
                      year January 1 to December 31, 2025.


                      2025 NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


                      2025 Non-NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


                      Back to Top ▲


                      Next Section


                      Continue


                      Reporting Change in Certain Individuals


                      Pursuant to the following sections of the New York Banking Law
                      (BL) and Superintendent’s Regulations (SR), licensees of the
                      Department of Financial Services (DFS) are required to notify
                      the Superintendent of changes in certain individuals, within
                      stipulated time frames:


                      Money Transmitters: BL 641, 642 and 652-a; and SR 406.11


                      These requirements are for changes in certain individuals of
                      licensees whose licenses are not managed on NMLS. For those
                      managed on NMLS, visit the NMLS section website for New York
                      State and navigate to Company Licenses and Amendment under the
                      pertinent industry type, and look under Change in Control on
                      the Amendment Checklist.


                      Included Individuals


                      Members of the governing board such as directors, trustees,
                      and LLC members


                      Officers (at a minimum Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief
                      Financial Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Operations
                      Officer, and any other officers deemed necessary by DFS)


                      Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being
                      Added


                      Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized
                      officer containing the following:


                      Name and title of the individual being added


                      Effective date of the addition


                      Name and title of the person being replaced, and his/her new
                      title/position, if any


                      Resolution of the governing board approving the addition


                      Personal Questionnaire (PDF)


                      Fingerprints


                      Background Investigation Report *


                      Litigation Affidavit (PDF)


                      Authority to Release Information (PDF)


                      Resume


                      Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being
                      Removed:


                      Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized
                      officer containing the following:


                      Name and title of the individual being removed


                      Reason of the removal


                      Effective date of the removal


                      New title/position, if any


                      Where To Submit?'

                    text: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S.


                      Published Date  January 29, 2026


                      To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo
                      a rigorous application process that involves dual compliance
                      with federal (like FinCEN''s AML/KYC protocols) and varying
                      state-level regulations. Key requirements across states include
                      demonstrating financial viability, often requiring a surety
                      bond and capital reserves, passing comprehensive background
                      checks for key personnel, and establishing a robust internal
                      compliance program. The process is complex, time-consuming,
                      and mandates extensive documentation and financial disclosures
                      to ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially sound.


                      Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling
                      a myriad of federal and state laws, making how to get a money
                      transmitter license both time-consuming and expensive. Compliance
                      with agencies like FinCEN is non-negotiable to prevent illegal
                      activities.


                      Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner
                      with a licensed entity, but legal adherence is vital in both
                      scenarios. It''s essential to understand what a money transmitter
                      license is and who needs it.


                      What is a Money Transmitter License?


                      A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or
                      money service business license that empowers a firm or individual
                      to facilitate the movement of capital. This license enables
                      MSBs to handle financial transactions, ranging from digital
                      payments to wire transfers.


                      Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial
                      regulatory oversight. Organizations must prove they have the
                      governance structure and internal controls to manage and safeguard
                      client funds. States will continually scrutinize applicants,
                      denying licensure to those who fail to meet the stringent criteria.


                      In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License
                      is not a choice; it''s a requirement for virtually any business
                      involved in the handling or transferring of funds. Money transmitter
                      license requirements by state can vary, so it''s crucial to
                      be aware of the respective state money transmitter regulations.


                      How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


                      The license application process is designed to be rigorous,
                      ensuring that approved businesses are law-abiding and financially
                      sound. Federal and state-level regulations diverge, with each
                      state setting its own financial criteria and often requiring
                      a minimum capital commitment.


                      Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000
                      per state, with costs influenced by credit history. The duration
                      to obtain the license varies, contingent on the business type
                      and the state of operation.


                      Money Transmitter License Requirements


                      Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with
                      Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols.
                      While these regulations are federal, individual states often
                      impose additional requirements, thereby necessitating dual compliance.


                      Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake
                      an investigative review, focusing on financial sustainability
                      and the applicant''s background.


                      Standardized Requirements Across States


                      Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the
                      Financial Crimes Enforcement Network or a similar state-level
                      body.'

                    text: ', 2026


                      Posted in Bank Regulatory


                      On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
                      issued a significant interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity
                      Digital Assets, National Association (the recently converted
                      national trust bank formerly known as Fidelity Digital Assets
                      Service, LLC) is not required to hold state money transmitter
                      licenses to conduct its federally authorized activities. The
                      OCC concluded that the National Bank Act preempts any state
                      money transmitter licensing requirement as applied to a national
                      bank.


                      Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as
                      a New York-chartered limited liability trust company and held
                      money transmitter licenses in numerous states, including Iowa.
                      On that date, the OCC approved its conversion to an uninsured
                      national trust bank under 12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent with
                      the conversion, the Bank surrendered its Iowa money transmitter
                      license.


                      Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks
                      and trust companies from licensing, but only if they hold federally
                      insured deposits. Because Fidelity Digital Assets is an uninsured
                      national bank, Iowa argued the exemption did not apply and requested
                      a legal basis for the license surrender. Fidelity Digital Assets
                      responded that the National Bank Act preempts Iowa’s requirements
                      and asked the OCC to confirm that position.


                      The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national
                      bank to obtain a state money transmitter license as a condition
                      of engaging in federally authorized activities, including cryptocurrency
                      custody, trade execution, stablecoin issuance, and related digital
                      asset services, rested on two independent and well-established
                      pillars of federal banking law:


                      1. National Bank Act Preemption


                      Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range
                      of activities on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents
                      or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s exercise
                      of its federally authorized powers is preempted.


                      The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a
                      state money transmitter license, even as a threshold condition
                      to operating, would impermissibly condition the Bank’s federal
                      authority on state approval. At the extreme, a state could veto
                      federal authority outright by denying or revoking a license.
                      Both outcomes are squarely preempted. This conclusion applies
                      to any state’s money transmitter licensing regime, including
                      states that limit their licensing exemptions to a subset of
                      national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only carveout).


                      2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


                      Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial
                      authority over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject
                      to any visitorial powers except as authorized by Federal law.”
                      Iowa’s money transmitter statute grants the state agency robust
                      supervisory jurisdiction over licensees, including the power
                      to demand books and records, conduct periodic examinations,
                      take enforcement actions, and even place a licensee into receivership.
                      Applying that regime to a national bank would be “fundamentally
                      inconsistent” with the OCC’s exclusive visitorial powers and
                      is therefore impermissible on independent grounds.


                      Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion:
                      a national bank may conduct its federally authorized activities
                      in any state without a state money transmitter license, regardless
                      of whether it qualifies for any state-law exemption.


                      Our Take


                      The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption
                      framework for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s
                      letter largely restates principles the Supreme Court and federal
                      courts have applied for decades. That said, one nuance in this
                      letter deserves closer attention: state-chartered trust banks
                      are in a very different position.


                      Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered
                      banks do not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their
                      ability to avoid state money transmitter licensing requirements
                      depends entirely on how each individual state defines “bank”
                      or “trust company” in its money transmission statute and those
                      definitions vary considerably.

              available_excerpt: "22 \n \n(e) \nWhen an application for acquisition

                not \nprohibited from acquiring control. \n(3) \nThe [Commissioner]
                may for good cause extend the application \nperiod. \n(f) \nA determination
                by the [Commissioner] that an application is complete and \nis accepted
                for processing means only that the application, on its face, appears

                are required, and is not an assessment of the substance of \nthe application
                or of the sufficiency of the information provided. \n(g) \nWhen an

                and business \nexperience, competence, character, and general fitness

                acquire control; and the competence, experience, character, \nand
                general fitness of the key individuals and persons that would be in

                that it is in the interest of the public to \npermit the person, or

                \nIf an applicant avails itself or is otherwise subject to a multistate
                licensing \n \n15 Commentary: NMLS will accommodate and streamline
                the process of communicating when applications are \nreceived and
                when states consider them to have been complete. The intent of this
                Act is for the application period to \nbegin on the day an application
                is determined to be complete.\n"

              available_excerpt: "23 \n \nprocess: \n(1) \nthe [Commissioner] is authorized

                state for the purpose of [Section 6.01(g)] if the \nlead investigative
                state has sufficient staffing, expertise, and minimum standards; or
                \n(2) \nif [state] is a lead investigative state, the [Commissioner]
                is \nauthorized and encouraged to investigate the applicant pursuant
                to [Section 6.01(g)] and \nthe timeframes established by agreement
                through the multistate licensing process. \n(i) \nThe [Commissioner]
                shall issue a formal written notice of the denial of an \napplication
                to acquire control within thirty (30) days of the decision to deny
                the application. The \n[Commissioner] shall set forth in the notice
                of denial the specific reasons for the denial of the \napplication.
                An applicant whose application is denied by the [Commissioner] under
                this [Section \n6.01(i)] may appeal within thirty (30) days16 after
                receipt of the written notice of the denial \n[pursuant to state administrative
                law procedures]. \n(j) \nThe requirements of [Section 6.01(a) and
                (b)] do not apply to any of the \nfollowing: \n(1) \nA person that
                acts as a proxy for the sole purpose of voting at a \ndesignated meeting
                of the shareholders or holders of voting shares or voting interests
                of a \nlicensee or a person in control of a licensee; \n(2) \nA person
                that acquires control of a licensee by devise or descent; \n(3) \nA
                person that acquires control of a licensee as a personal \nrepresentative,
                custodian, guardian, conservator, or trustee, or as an officer appointed
                by a \ncourt of competent jurisdiction or by operation of law; \n(4)
                \nA person that is exempt under [Section 3.01(g)]; \n(5) \nA person
                that the [Commissioner] determines is not subject to \n[Section 6.01(a)]
                based on the public interest; \n(6) \nA public offering of securities
                of a licensee or a person in control of \na licensee; or \n(7) \nAn
                internal reorganization of a person in control of the licensee \nwhere
                the ultimate person in control of the licensee remains the same. \n(k)
                \nPersons in [Sections 6.01(j)(2), (3), (4), (6), (7)] in cooperation
                with the \nlicensee shall notify the [Commissioner] within [15] days
                after the acquisition of control.17 \n \n16 Commentary: Administrative
                procedures for challenging a departmental decision may be derived
                from other \naspects of state law. In such a case, this Act should

                power to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 25 percent of \nthe
                outstanding voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person
                in control of a \nlicensee; \n(B) \nthe power to elect or appoint
                a majority of key individuals or \nexecutive officers, managers, directors,

                directly or indirectly, a controlling \ninfluence over the management
                or policies of a licensee or person in control of a \nlicensee. \n(2)
                \nRebuttable Presumption of Control. \n(A) \nA person is presumed
                to exercise a controlling influence \nwhen the person holds the power
                to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 10 percent \nof the outstanding
                voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person in control
                \nof a licensee.2 \n(B) \nA person presumed to exercise a controlling
                influence as \ndefined by this [Section 2.01(f)] can rebut the presumption
                of control if the person \nis a passive investor. \n(3) \nFor purposes
                of determining the percentage of a person controlled \nby any other
                person, the person's interest shall be aggregated with the interest
                of any other \nimmediate family member, including the person's spouse,
                parents, children, siblings, \nmothers- and fathers-in law, sons-
                and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law, and \nany other
                person who shares such person's home. \n(g) \n\"Eligible rating\"
                shall mean a credit rating of any of the three highest rating \ncategories
                provided by an eligible rating service, whereby each category may
                include rating \n \n2 Commentary: The obligation to rebut control
                rests exclusively with the person acquiring ≥10% of the outstanding
                \nvoting shares or voting interests of a licensee or person in control
                of a licensee.  It is not the responsibility of the \nlicensee to
                rebut control.  This is consistent with Section 601(a) of the Act
                which requires the person acquiring control \nto obtain prior approval.\n"

                \n(c) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money in trust for the benefit

                \n(d) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money in trust for the benefit

              unit_id: s000001
              locator: Section 1, characters 2400–7324
              available_excerpt: 'ey Transmitter License.


                Access to NMLS


                NMLS is a secure web-based system created by state regulators to provide
                efficiencies in the processing of state licenses and improve supervision
                of state-regulated industries.


                To access NMLS for the first time, you must complete a Company Account
                Request Form and identify a Primary Account Administrator and a Secondary
                Account Administrator. This form can be submitted online through the
                NMLS website in the Getting Started section. This form needs to be
                submitted only once per company, regardless of the number of NMLS
                participating states in which you are licensed.


                Within three days of completing and submitting the Company Account
                Request Form, the Primary Account Administrator will receive NMLS
                login information. The Primary Account Administrator will have full
                rights to access the system, submit information to this agency and
                other participating state regulators, and set up other company users
                in the system. Instructions and tutorials on how to access and use
                the system are also available in the NMLS Resource Center .


                Note : If your company already has a record in NMLS, you can omit
                this step.


                Managing Your License on NMLS


                Each company holding a DFS Money Transmitter License who wishes to
                manage their license on NMLS must create a company record in the system.
                To gain access to NMLS, the applicant must submit a form requesting
                an NMLS account.


                Current New York State Money Transmitters may transition their licenses
                to NMLS. See the DFS Money Transmitter Transition Checklist for more
                information.


                Submitting a Complete Application


                To submit an application and ensure your application is received,
                acknowledged as complete, and processed, please follow the instructions
                on the DFS Money Transmitter Checklists . No application shall be
                deemed to be complete until the Department has received all required
                information, documents, and fees.


                In the process of reviewing and considering the application, DFS may
                request additional information and supporting documents.


                In the application process, an NMLS Identification Number will be
                assigned to your application. Please maintain a record of this NMLS
                Identification Number, as it will be used as your application reference
                number throughout the remainder of the application process. The applicant’s
                NMLS Identification Number must be included on every hard-copy document
                submitted to the Department.


                Note : If the applicant has already submitted Forms MU1 and MU2 through
                NMLS for another state, the applicant does not need to re-enter the
                company record into NMLS. However, the applicant is required to provide
                jurisdiction-specific information to support its New York State application.


                Back to Top ▲


                Next Section


                Continue


                Annual Reporting


                The Annual Report should be prepared by qualified persons and submitted
                within 120 days following the close of the calendar year January 1
                to December 31, 2025.


                2025 NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


                2025 Non-NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


                Back to Top ▲


                Next Section


                Continue


                Reporting Change in Certain Individuals


                Pursuant to the following sections of the New York Banking Law (BL)
                and Superintendent’s Regulations (SR), licensees of the Department
                of Financial Services (DFS) are required to notify the Superintendent
                of changes in certain individuals, within stipulated time frames:


                Money Transmitters: BL 641, 642 and 652-a; and SR 406.11


                These requirements are for changes in certain individuals of licensees
                whose licenses are not managed on NMLS. For those managed on NMLS,
                visit the NMLS section website for New York State and navigate to
                Company Licenses and Amendment under the pertinent industry type,
                and look under Change in Control on the Amendment Checklist.


                Included Individuals


                Members of the governing board such as directors, trustees, and LLC
                members


                Officers (at a minimum Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief Financial
                Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Operations Officer, and
                any other officers deemed necessary by DFS)


                Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Added


                Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized
                officer containing the following:


                Name and title of the individual being added


                Effective date of the addition


                Name and title of the person being replaced, and his/her new title/position,
                if any


                Resolution of the governing board approving the addition


                Personal Questionnaire (PDF)


                Fingerprints


                Background Investigation Report *


                Litigation Affidavit (PDF)


                Authority to Release Information (PDF)


                Resume


                Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Removed:


                Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized
                officer containing the following:


                Name and title of the individual being removed


                Reason of the removal


                Effective date of the removal


                New title/position, if any

              source_hash: b8cfb71cc698f4b53cce08d023441fce54bf275adbcb1164dfb05a05143f6ba9
              source_label: How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S.
                - Fenergo — Section 2, characters 0–3321
              unit_id: s000002
              locator: Section 2, characters 0–3321
              available_excerpt: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in
                the U.S.


                Published Date  January 29, 2026


                To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo
                a rigorous application process that involves dual compliance with
                federal (like FinCEN''s AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level
                regulations. Key requirements across states include demonstrating
                financial viability, often requiring a surety bond and capital reserves,
                passing comprehensive background checks for key personnel, and establishing
                a robust internal compliance program. The process is complex, time-consuming,
                and mandates extensive documentation and financial disclosures to
                ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially sound.


                Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling a
                myriad of federal and state laws, making how to get a money transmitter
                license both time-consuming and expensive. Compliance with agencies
                like FinCEN is non-negotiable to prevent illegal activities.


                Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with
                a licensed entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios.
                It''s essential to understand what a money transmitter license is
                and who needs it.


                What is a Money Transmitter License?


                A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money
                service business license that empowers a firm or individual to facilitate
                the movement of capital. This license enables MSBs to handle financial
                transactions, ranging from digital payments to wire transfers.


                Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial regulatory
                oversight. Organizations must prove they have the governance structure
                and internal controls to manage and safeguard client funds. States
                will continually scrutinize applicants, denying licensure to those
                who fail to meet the stringent criteria.


                In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License is
                not a choice; it''s a requirement for virtually any business involved
                in the handling or transferring of funds. Money transmitter license
                requirements by state can vary, so it''s crucial to be aware of the
                respective state money transmitter regulations.


                How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


                The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring
                that approved businesses are law-abiding and financially sound. Federal
                and state-level regulations diverge, with each state setting its own
                financial criteria and often requiring a minimum capital commitment.


                Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per state,
                with costs influenced by credit history. The duration to obtain the
                license varies, contingent on the business type and the state of operation.


                Money Transmitter License Requirements


                Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with Anti-Money
                Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols. While these
                regulations are federal, individual states often impose additional
                requirements, thereby necessitating dual compliance.


                Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake
                an investigative review, focusing on financial sustainability and
                the applicant''s background.


                Standardized Requirements Across States


                Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial
                Crimes Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

              url: https://www.troutmanfinancialservices.com/2026/06/occ-confirms-national-bank-act-preempts-state-money-transmitter-licensing-for-fidelity-digital-assets/
              original_path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/RUN-20260911-d08e84-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413-fetch.md.bin
              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413/e06621859d4ec9431f2712a7c357b112/sections/s000001.md
              source_hash: 8ef30c0b98621db1f11c16332c16e9928ea8f237d6b055f645f7b449f18cbdfb
              source_label: OCC Confirms National Bank Act Preempts State Money Transmitter
                ... — Section 1, characters 600–4794
              unit_id: s000001
              locator: Section 1, characters 600–4794
              available_excerpt: ', 2026


                Posted in Bank Regulatory


                On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued
                a significant interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity Digital
                Assets, National Association (the recently converted national trust
                bank formerly known as Fidelity Digital Assets Service, LLC) is not
                required to hold state money transmitter licenses to conduct its federally
                authorized activities. The OCC concluded that the National Bank Act
                preempts any state money transmitter licensing requirement as applied
                to a national bank.


                Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a New
                York-chartered limited liability trust company and held money transmitter
                licenses in numerous states, including Iowa. On that date, the OCC
                approved its conversion to an uninsured national trust bank under
                12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent with the conversion, the Bank surrendered
                its Iowa money transmitter license.


                Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks and
                trust companies from licensing, but only if they hold federally insured
                deposits. Because Fidelity Digital Assets is an uninsured national
                bank, Iowa argued the exemption did not apply and requested a legal
                basis for the license surrender. Fidelity Digital Assets responded
                that the National Bank Act preempts Iowa’s requirements and asked
                the OCC to confirm that position.


                The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national bank
                to obtain a state money transmitter license as a condition of engaging
                in federally authorized activities, including cryptocurrency custody,
                trade execution, stablecoin issuance, and related digital asset services,
                rested on two independent and well-established pillars of federal
                banking law:


                1. National Bank Act Preemption


                Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range of
                activities on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents or significantly
                interferes” with a national bank’s exercise of its federally authorized
                powers is preempted.


                The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state
                money transmitter license, even as a threshold condition to operating,
                would impermissibly condition the Bank’s federal authority on state
                approval. At the extreme, a state could veto federal authority outright
                by denying or revoking a license. Both outcomes are squarely preempted.
                This conclusion applies to any state’s money transmitter licensing
                regime, including states that limit their licensing exemptions to
                a subset of national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only carveout).


                2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


                Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial
                authority over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject
                to any visitorial powers except as authorized by Federal law.” Iowa’s
                money transmitter statute grants the state agency robust supervisory
                jurisdiction over licensees, including the power to demand books and
                records, conduct periodic examinations, take enforcement actions,
                and even place a licensee into receivership. Applying that regime
                to a national bank would be “fundamentally inconsistent” with the
                OCC’s exclusive visitorial powers and is therefore impermissible on
                independent grounds.


                Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion:
                a national bank may conduct its federally authorized activities in
                any state without a state money transmitter license, regardless of
                whether it qualifies for any state-law exemption.


                Our Take


                The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption framework
                for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter largely restates
                principles the Supreme Court and federal courts have applied for decades.
                That said, one nuance in this letter deserves closer attention: state-chartered
                trust banks are in a very different position.


                Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered banks
                do not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their ability to
                avoid state money transmitter licensing requirements depends entirely
                on how each individual state defines “bank” or “trust company” in
                its money transmission statute and those definitions vary considerably.

                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-db6468aeb552bb44aa7b.md
                  revision: 916b7009f261c21b7029be2ac4bab07fb4fd2909920244882bc8c02250c75dac

                  passages: &id141
                  - start: 0
                    end: 1441
                    text: '# Issues and workstreams


                      - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
                      under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s
                      MTLs transfer/survive the acquisition

                      - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with
                      missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic
                      Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations

                      - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
                      Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

                      - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
                      when the SaaS contract terminates at close

                      - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any
                      state money transmission or consumer protection implications

                      - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!--
                      issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06 -->

                      - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition
                      diligence <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

                      - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase
                      <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf -->

                      - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2
                      -->

                      - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
                      -->

                      - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
                      -->

                      - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus
                      <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481 -->

                      '
                  source_version: 916b7009f261c21b7029be2ac4bab07fb4fd2909920244882bc8c02250c75dac

                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c.md
                  revision: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

                  passages: &id142
                  - start: 0
                    end: 3962
                    text: '# Known Facts


                      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15
                      (~10 weeks out).

                      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                      into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified
                      account and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d
                      by Harbor.

                      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states;
                      Mosaic Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening
                      four new markets.

                      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024;
                      Mosaic has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying
                      documents for users onboarded before 2023.

                      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose
                      contract terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction
                      feed at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on
                      first transfer, launching close+1.

                      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs
                      from the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                      into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified
                      account and balance.

                      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor
                      users were already KYC''d.

                      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024;
                      pass/fail results exist for everyone but underlying documents
                      are missing for users onboarded before 2023.

                      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose
                      contract terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction
                      feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs
                      from the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                      (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                      on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification,
                      or is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with
                      compliance

                      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs
                      from the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint,
                      does Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses
                      or apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                      what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                      identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet
                      known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance
                      on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the
                      last year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open
                      alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in
                      diligence.

                      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                      what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                      before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently
                      plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                      ## Assumptions


                      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                      and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                      the acquisition without new state approval

                      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                      Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the
                      underlying documents

                      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                      and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                      to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet
                      confirmed).

                      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                      in 41 states (per the request).

                      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or
                      stock purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and
                      SAR/alert obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                      '
                  source_version: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

              path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/sources/SRC-LOCAL-5b01121f7bfd7357746c.md
              original_path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md
              title: facts.md
              support_state: supplied
              source_type: workspace
              available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


                - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                weeks out).

                - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into
                Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by
                Harbor.

                - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                markets.

                - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                for users onboarded before 2023.

                - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed
                at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                transfer, launching close+1.

                - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into
                Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                and balance.

                - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users
                were already KYC''d.

                - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
                results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for
                users onboarded before 2023.

                - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic
                Relay''s engine on day 1.

                - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic
                buys Harbor''s assets)

                - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on
                another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification
                required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

                - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from
                the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does
                Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or
                apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification
                and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic
                Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC;
                compliance must confirm.

                - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year
                been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR
                history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

                - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans
                to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                ## Assumptions


                - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through the
                acquisition without new state approval

                - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying
                documents

                - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

                - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                in 41 states (per the request).

                - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock
                purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations
                transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                '

                  title: State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase
                  why_it_matters: The migration plan assumes Harbor’s licenses will
                    permit service in four new markets. An asset purchase might not
                    transfer those licenses or their operating authority to Mosaic.
                  parent_issue_id: null
                  fact_ids: []
                  disposition: null
                questions:
                - question_id: Q-SAR
                  text: Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the
                    last year been reviewed, and what did they reveal?
                  consequence: Unread open alerts and SARs are the highest-risk item;
                    they can create BSA/AML exposure that must be addressed before
                    close and could affect the deal itself.
                  state: answered
                  answer: The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed and
                    remain in diligence.
                  answer_kind: reported_fact
                  linked_fact_ids:
                  - FACT-20260909-070aec
                - question_id: Q-KYC
                  text: For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                    what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay's own BSA/AML customer
                    identification and recordkeeping obligations?
                  consequence: Whether the missing underlying documents create a compliance
                    gap depends on how Mosaic plans to satisfy its own CIP/recordkeeping
                    obligations for these users.
                  state: answered
                  answer: It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay's AML/CIP program
                    permits reliance on Harbor's prior KYC; compliance must confirm.
                  answer_kind: reported_fact
                  linked_fact_ids:
                  - FACT-20260909-620c62
                - question_id: Q-MTL
                  text: For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                    what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                    before onboarding those customers?
                  consequence: Whether the four new markets can be served at close
                    depends on license transferability and state approval, which is
                    a gating regulatory question.
                  state: answered
                  answer: Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor's licenses
                    for the four new markets.
                  answer_kind: reported_fact
                  linked_fact_ids:
                  - FACT-20260909-771ee1
                - question_id: Q-BONUS
                  text: How is the $50 welcome bonus structured?
                  consequence: The structure determines whether the bonus triggers
                    consumer disclosure, funds-flow, or state promotional requirements.

                  - start: 0
                    end: 3962
                    text: '# Known Facts


                      - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15
                      (~10 weeks out).

                      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                      into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified
                      account and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                      - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d
                      by Harbor.

                      - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states;
                      Mosaic Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening
                      four new markets.

                      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024;
                      Mosaic has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying
                      documents for users onboarded before 2023.

                      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose
                      contract terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction
                      feed at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                      - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on
                      first transfer, launching close+1.

                      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs
                      from the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                      - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                      into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified
                      account and balance.

                      - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor
                      users were already KYC''d.

                      - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024;
                      pass/fail results exist for everyone but underlying documents
                      are missing for users onboarded before 2023.

                      - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose
                      contract terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction
                      feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                      - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs
                      from the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                      - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                      (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                      - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                      on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification,
                      or is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with
                      compliance

                      - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs
                      from the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                      - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint,
                      does Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses
                      or apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                      - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                      what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                      identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet
                      known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance
                      on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                      - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the
                      last year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open
                      alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in
                      diligence.

                      - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                      what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                      before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently
                      plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                      ## Assumptions


                      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                      and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                      the acquisition without new state approval

                      - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                      Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the
                      underlying documents

                      - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                      and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                      - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                      to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet
                      confirmed).

                      - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                      in 41 states (per the request).

                      - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or
                      stock purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and
                      SAR/alert obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                      '
                  source_version: 58b0379461c2b3d9c58807fff3ac3f7136d5aedd4f20022fc8be9eeb64cec409

                  - start: 0

                    text: '# Issues and workstreams


                      - Money transmission licensing: whether Mosaic Relay can operate
                      under the combined 44-state footprint and whether Harbor''s
                      MTLs transfer/survive the acquisition

                      - BSA/AML and KYC: whether relying on Harbor''s prior KYC (with
                      missing underlying documents for pre-2023 users) satisfies Mosaic
                      Relay''s independent CIP/AML obligations

                      - SAR and alert handling: obligations to review, file, and manage
                      Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and SARs, and successor liability

                      - Monitoring vendor transition: continuity of transaction monitoring
                      when the SaaS contract terminates at close

                      - Marketing compliance: the $50 welcome bonus offer and any
                      state money transmission or consumer protection implications

                      - Customer account, contract, and data-transfer rights <!--
                      issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-af341445a7af4c06 -->

                      - Open alerts, suspicious activity history, and acquisition
                      diligence <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-d22ea3957f21252a -->

                      - State money-transmission authority after the asset purchase
                      <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-65ae94508dcda1bf -->

                      - Reliance on Harbor’s prior identity verification <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-30caa16a9234ccf2
                      -->

                      - Transaction-monitoring continuity at cutover <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-1d13a6636b8fbe60
                      -->

                      - Purchase-agreement authority and risk allocation <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-29efc151650e76a2
                      -->

                      - Customer terms, privacy, data transfers, and welcome bonus
                      <!-- issue:ISS-c9d7c39f63-fcd3954739e05481 -->

                      '
